heading: Abstract:
content: Final Year Project (FYP) reports are frequently a very tedious and professional writing where students have to adhere to specific guidelines of the institutions. Formatting by hand takes up precious time, and distracts the actual research, and often the issue of inconsistencies ensues. The current project suggests creating an AI-driven Report Formatter that will automate the process of formatting the reports, making sure they are formatted in accordance with the institution-specific template and protecting the academic integrity. The system uses Natural Language Processing (NLP) and machine learning to identify the elements of a document (headings, paragraphs, tables, figures and references) and uses these elements to apply formatting rules. An exclusive administration panel will enable the institutions to post and maintain their own templates to guarantee a high level of flexibility in the various universities. The innovations are AI-based with ethical vs. unethical image detection, which filters indecent or otherwise unacademic images, and a voice-activated formatting interface, which lets the user set formatting instructions by simply speaking to the computer and improving accessibility. Other functions provided are plagiarism and grammar check, absent section suggestions, and live preview. Word, PDF and LaTeX export options will be used to provide a high number of compatibility. The proposed solution alleviates the administrative workload of formatting, enhances academic integrity and increases accessibility in students by incorporating smart content classification and ethical protection as well as multi-modal interaction with users. In the end, the Report Formatter hopes to be a smart academic assistant that fills the gap between the creation of content and the presentation of the professional work, thus contributing to the high level of productivity and the quality of academic work in general.

heading: Background
content: Report writing is part and parcel of academic and professional work. In tertiary education, learners have to deliver reports, theses, and project documentation which has to be in perfect format according to the requirements that are given by their institutions of higher learning. Such formatting guidelines usually include font types, font size, headings hierarchy, margin requirements, table format, reference format and other organizational aspects. Although these standards are required to ensure uniformity and readability, the manual formatting is normally time consuming, difficult and cannot be done without errors. Students are often wasted in matching headings, numbering lists and the reference styles more than in the actual content of their work. The latter is even more difficult when the various institutions have varying formatting standards. As an example, one university might recommend using the APA style form of reference, and another one to use IEEE or Chicago style. Equally, the specifications on the appearance of the table, the position of the caption and the structure of the sections can be quite diverse. This is because the absence of a universal tool that can adapt to various formatting needs makes compliance quite challenging to the students, and in fact, unintentional non-compliance to institutional standards can be experienced. These difficulties are intensified in other group projects, where several contributors join their parts together in one document and in most instances the parts do not match. Moreover, in the contemporary digital reports, figures and images may occasionally be included. Nevertheless, uncontrolled insertion of unethical or unacceptable images may affect academic integrity. In this way, not only do the quality of the content have to be properly formatted, but also the possibility to avoid the incorporation of unethical content into the academic records. As automation, artificial intelligence, and natural language processing become increasingly more dependable, there is a high demand on a smart solution that can automatize formatting, comply with ethical standards, and offer an opportunity to allow the user to define the formatting needs in flexible ways.

heading: Problem Statement
content: The existing procedure of report creating is ineffective, prone to errors, and does not help the students to concentrate on their research quality. The vast majority of students do not have the technical knowledge to work with the more advanced formatting features of programs like Microsoft word or LaTeX. Consequently, they have to use manual adjustments that are quite repetitive and in most cases result in wastage of time, stress, and inconsistency of formatting. Moreover, the lack of an automated program that can address various institutional needs has presented a barrier to students who study in various academic settings. Another problem that keeps on reoccurring in a collaborative environment is the ability to merge various sections without losing formatting. Insufficiency of mechanisms used to guarantee ethical contents is another cause of concern. Learners will either add unprofessional images in their reports without knowing how, or they can do it deliberately, and this can result in both academic and professional punishment. Furthermore, the existing systems restrict the formatting to the manual mode of input and they do not consider innovations like speech-based instructions, which might make the process more user-friendly with people with varying needs. Therefore, an urgent demand is seen in the creation of the system that will be not only automated in formatting but also will make use of artificial intelligence to sort, arrange, and ethically control the material and promote various forms of interaction with the users.

heading: Proposed Solution
content: The offered project, which will be called Report Formatter, presents an AI- and machine learning-based program that will be used to automate the process of report formatting based on the templates specified by the user or institutions. The system will include: Admin Panel: It allows administrators to post and control format regulations like font styles, margins, table formats and heading structures. A custom template can be done by each university. AI-Powered Content Classification: Detecting attributes (heading, subheading, tables, images, captions, references) and formats them accordingly Ethical Image Detection: The system incorporates an AI model, which is capable of differentiating between ethical and unethical images. In case of an inappropriate or unethical image posted, the system will make sure that it is not included in the report, thus making sure that one does not go against academic and professional standards. Voice-Enabled Formatting Requirements: The users and administrators will be able to set formatting requirements by speech recognition using a microphone. This natural language processing capability renders the system more usable and easy to use especially when the user finds it more comfortable or needs to use voice interactivity as opposed to using handwriting. Student Application: This will enable students to post raw data (Word, PDF or plain text) and get a well formatted report according to the template of their campus. Specialized: Grammar checking, plagiarism checking, table of contents auto-generated, audio and table numbering, section recognition, version control, collaboration, and multilingual. Security Measures: It has data security and privacy measures which have been incorporated in order to secure sensitive academic work with the use of encryption and local storage. There is also live preview, with students being able to see changes in formatting on the fly, just like on platforms like LaTeX like Overleaf. Combining all these features, the solution is expected to offer a complete platform that is not confined to mere formatting and can improve the academic writing overall.

heading: Expected Outcomes
content: Application of Report Formatter system should bring about some gains: Time Savings: The automation of the repetitive format process will save the students much time so that they can be able to spend the time on creating the content and conducting research. Consistency and Accuracy: With automated formatting, the problem of human error will be removed, and the strict adherence to the requirements of the institution will be ensured. Ethical Protections: The unethical image detection feature can be used to keep academic reports professional, ethical and devoid of unprofessional content. Increased Accessibility - Speech-based input should allow users to create formatting rules via the voice, which will make the system more inclusive and easier to use. Improved Quality: Grammar correction and plagiarism detector features will help in bettering the quality and originality of reports. Collaboration Support: Teamwork in academic projects will be simplified with such features as version control and collaboration between people. Flexibility and Adaptability: The system will support the different formatting rules and languages and therefore can be applicable across the various institutions and regions. Flexibility: Compatibility with other academic submissions platforms, such as Word, PDF, and LaTeX document export capabilities will make it flexible. Data Security: Vigorous privacy protocols will ensure that sensitive student reports are safe and they are not abused. The purpose of this Report Formatter is, finally, to become a smart assistant to the students, researchers and institutions by creating a linkage between the content development, ethical adherence and professionalism. Using artificial intelligence, the system will not only enhance effectiveness of report writing, but also establish new levels of academic productivity, inclusiveness, and quality.

heading: Related Work:
content: Document formatting automation is a new discipline that touches on Natural Language Processing (NLP), document layout analysis, and rule-based systems. Various commercial and academic solutions have tried to solve sections of this issue, but there exists little in the way of a widespread, template-driven, AI-assisted, academic report solution. Commercial word processors Powerful in their styling capabilities and templates, Microsoft Word and Google Docs need to be used manually. They are not smart enough to guess the framework of the unstructured academic text. Users have to apply formatting, which creates errors and inconsistency in longer reports. Overleaf and LaTeX In academia, Overleaf, a LaTeX cloud-based editor, is being widely used due to its strong typesetting features and active collaboration functionality [1]. Nevertheless, it involves the user learning how to use LaTeX, an important barrier to entry to many non-technical students. Although it is the best at generating well-structured reports, it does not offer AI flexibility in response to customer requirements. AI-driven text models GPT-based models, including ChatGPT, are able to produce and occasionally organize text but not be used to adhere to more complicated text formatting conventions, including margins, page breaks, or caption position. They also do not have a specific pipeline of analyzing document layout and adherence to formatting. Document Layout Analysis (DLA) DLA research is very relevant. Some projects like LayoutLM (Microsoft) [2] and DocBank [3] are based on deep learning to recognize textual and visual characteristics to understand the structure of the documents (titles, authors, paragraphs, etc.). These models are the basis of technology of our classification module but are research oriented as opposed to being implemented as end user academic tools. Content quality tools Grammatically and Turnitin are adjacent solutions. Grammarly prioritizes grammar, clarity, and tone recommendations [4] whereas Turnitin is the default plagiarism detection engine in the industry [5]. Nevertheless, both of them do not offer automatic formatting and adherence to institutional templates. Template engines Document creation systems such as Jinja or Apache POI are programmatic methods of document creation, where template documents are filled in with information. They are helpful with automation but not adaptive because they are unable to process unstructured academic material intelligently and correlate it with templates without human-defined rules. Automated format research A prototype of an NLP-based formatting system, which can be used to process documents and execute some rules automatically, was described by Islam & Rahman (2022) [6]. Although this is proof of its feasibility, the model is not extensible and fails to cover such sophisticated options as detecting ethics in images or speech-driven interaction. Ethical/unethical image detection Professional and academic integrity can be undermined by the uncontrolled incorporation of unethical or inappropriate pictures. Research in computer vision can be a good solution to this field. Image classification Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), ResNet, multimodal networks like CLIP [7] are examples of models that have been shown to have high precision in image classification tasks. Such systems are able to recognize inappropriate or irrelevant content and they are thus appropriate to be included in academic formatting software to maintain ethical standards. Speeches and voice interaction Speech recognition can be used to improve accessibility in formatting systems. The studies of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and intent classification, including Graves et al. (2006) [8], allow mapping natural speech to actions. New developments such as Google Speech-to-Text API and Whisper prove the accuracy of the transcription, and voice-powered formatting is possible and useful to the academic software with inclusivity. The project is expected to make an integration of all these disparate domains - DLA, NLP, template engines, computer vision, ASR and writing assistance tools into one user friendly application that is specifically tailored to an academic scenario, which currently there is a gap in the existing ecosystem of writing tools.

heading: Architecture
content: The architecture of the AI-based FYP Report Formatter is represented in this diagram (Figure 1), as well as the interaction between its key components. The system has four major components: Frontend (Desktop Application): Students utilize a cross-platform desktop use that has been developed on Flutter. They are able to view the ready output and post unrefined report material. Templates are also controlled by the administrators using the frontend. Backend (Python and AI Models): Supervises claims of formatting, plagiarism, and grammar, assignments categorization and AI-inspired propositions. Database (PostgreSQL): It holds in the PostgreSQL database; User data, version history, templates used to format data to different colleges, report data, which are scalable and satisfies the ACID. External Integrations: Exports both LaTeX/Pandoc to high quality and optional plagiarism APIs and AI categorization using spaCy and Hugging Face Transformers. The diagram describes these elements interaction by processing pipelines and API calls to achieve successful formatting and generation of reports.

heading: Methodology:
content: The report formatter is  developed with a structured pipeline to ensure that it is properly formatted and that the content of the reports is classified based on data AI to identify the essential elements of the report. The interconnecting modules constituting the architecture (Figure 1) are each with a unique purpose. 1. Admin Panel Module: This module defines formatting templates, such as margins, table styles, placement of captions, hierarchy of headings, font size, and style. The templates are stored in the Template Database. 2. User Module(Students): This module handles registration, logins and submission of reports by students. It provides file upload services of text, PDF, and word documents. 3. File Upload and Parsing Module: It receives uploaded files and removes their raw content (text, tables and figures) and converts the information into a structured format to enable AI to process it. 4. AI Content Classification Module: The NLP model marks the sections (Heading 1, Heading 2, paragraphs, tables, photos, captions, references, etc.) of the text. It provides the Formatting Engine with directed content. 5. Formatting Engine Module: It uses standards of the university template to a content that is categorised and controls captions, margins, spacing, numbering and styles of headers. A draft report is generated. 6. Other AI Services: Plagiarism and grammar checker ensure the accuracy and originality. AI recommendations provides recommendations to missing portions of the paper, including the Conclusion. 7. Table of Contents/ Numbering Module: This will automatically generate a list of figures, list of tables and table of contents. It perfectly places captions (under the pictures, on the top of the tables). 8. Collaboration & Version Control Module: It allows a number of different students to post and merge sections. The rollback version history is also maintained. 9. Live Preview Module: It provides a preview of the organized report live. Students can see changes immediately, as it works with Overleaf. 10. Image Ethics Detection Module: This recognizes ethical or unethical images uploaded and beforehand inserts them, based on pre-trained computer vision models (e.g. ResNet, CLIP or custom CNNs). The moracious pictures pass, the immoral row. 11. Voice to Command Module: Speech recognition engine converts the spoken instructions into actions (e.g. bold heading, insert caption). It uses commands to format actions relying on ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition) and NLP intent-classification.

heading: Introduction
content: The Secure Message Platform designed to provide people a secure and reliable communication platform. Nowadays, where cyberattacks and data breaches are happening more often security is the main focus of everyone. So, there is a great demand of such communication platform where data remains safe. The solution is centered on combining strong security measures such as data encryption, user authentication and access control along with a simple and user friendly design. Our goal is to provide data security not only for an individual but also for enterprises and institutions that manage sensitive information.

heading: Advantages
content: Encryption across end-to-end (E2EE): The major advantage is that all communication (text, voice, video, documents) is encrypted. Only the sender and receiver are able to see / access the content and read / listen to these messages. The service provider cannot even see the communication. End-to-end encryption reduces the likelihood of hacking or data breaches. Sure Message Delivery:  Messages are not available or recognizable by third parties during their delivery. Integrity and Authenticity: Verification of the message as coming from the intended recipient and that it has not been changed using digital signatures or cryptology.

heading: Feature List
content: The feature list include ; End-to-end encrypted messaging, secure voice / video calling, image sharing with built-in encryption, voice messaging with encrypted audio recordings, user authentication (passwords, multi-factor login), secure file transfer between users.

heading: Objectives
content: The Objectives include; to design and develop a trustable and secure communication platform and to ensure data protection using the principles of confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA).

heading: Project Abstract
content: GoMate ride sharing app is created for users to get reliable and economic transportation.. GoMate offers two ride options: single-user rides and ridesharing. For single-user rides, GoMate is like any other ride booking service, where users can book a ride to their desired destination for single user rides. The unique ride-sharing feature allows two users to share a ride if their pickup locations are within a predefined radius or on the same route, decreasing the driver’s deviation. This ensures convenient and efficient journey for both. Fares are  calculated based on their routes. Real-time location tracking, a user-friendly interface, and efficient matching algorithms will be integrated to make the experience good for both riders and drivers. Users will also be able to send parcels across the city using a parcel delivery feature. To enable secure and smooth user experience, social logins and real time status updates will be integrated. GoMate offers a sustainable and scalable alternative in transportation, focusing on cities with rising demand for cost-effective shared transportation services.

heading: Introduction
content: GoMate aims to deliver a reliable, cost effective and user friendly solution for urban transportation.It is inspired by popular ride-booking services like Uber and Careem, but offers unique features that make travelling more convenient and more efficient. The app will serve a dual purpose: Users are offered the choice of booking either a private ride or a ride sharing option, in which they can share rides with others headed in the same direction. This ride-sharing feature will match users based on a proximity radius or route alignment, so that deviation from the original route is minimal for drivers. GoMate focuses on efficient route management and minimal driver detours, which will promise time and cost efficient solution for both riders and drivers. For users who want to send packages across the city, GoMate will also include an additional parcel delivery feature. The aim of this feature is to meet the increasing need for fast and flexible local delivery options. The development of GoMate involves multiple sub-tasks, which contribute to the app’s functionality and user experience. Many of the key sub-tasks include designing a scalable backend to handle complex ride-matching algorithms. Real time location tracking and route visualization will be provided by the app using Google Maps, with updates on the rider’s and driver’s positions in real time. Other components of the project involve developing a responsive frontend to provide a smooth user experience across both iOS and Android platforms.

heading: Success Criterion
content: The success of the GoMate will be determined by its ability to deliver a smooth, efficient and user-friendly ride sharing experience that meets its core capabilities. Success criteria are defined for GoMate to meet its usability, reliability and innovation objectives. The project will be deemed successful if it meets the following three criteria:

heading: Functional Completeness of Minimum Viable Product (MVP)
content: MVP is one of the key success criteria. The goal is to develop and deploy a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) that contains the main features of the GoMate application. This MVP will have ride booking for a single user, ride sharing, and parcel delivery feature.In order for the MVP to be successful, the user must be able to book a ride for themselves or share the ride with another passenger within a given radius. This initial version is intended to be user friendly and highly responsive so that it provides a good base for future improvements. This criterion will be verified through usability testing and user feedback.

heading: Real-Time Location Tracking and Ride-Matching Efficiency
content: Second success criterion is to integrate an accurate real-time location tracking with an effective ride-matching algorithm. These components are vital for GoMate to make the intended convenient and cost-efficient fulfillment. Using Google Maps, real time tracking will also be possible, hence users will monitor the driver’s location while on the ride as well as receive notifications regarding estimated time of arrival. The ride-matching algorithm will determine whether a second passenger can be picked up based on proximity and route alignment, ensuring minimal deviations for the driver. Success will be assessed based on the accuracy of location updates, matching algorithms, and their responsiveness in actual scenarios. This criterion will be tested under various conditions, such as peak usage, to ensure that the system can respond fast and efficiently under load.

heading: Positive User Feedback on Usability and Satisfaction
content: One of the major indicators of success of GoMate is to gain positive response from the end users regarding the ease of operation, the working of the application and the overall satisfaction level. This criterion recognizes that for this concept to be successful, it must be effective not only in terms of functionality but also in terms of how the users will find it. It is important that the user-interaction is seamless, users should be able to easily book a ride, track their driver and rides. Usability testing will be conducted which will involve a collection of data from sample users with regards to the app’s layout, performance to evaluate the response time, reliability and ease of use among others. GoMate will be deemed successful if there are positive comments from the users to support its efficient and interactive interface.

heading: Related Work
content: Some of the most famous apps with the concept of ride sharing have become leaders in their field, changing the transport services and providing the population with accessible and comfortable means of transport. Uber  has presented affordable and expensive versions of services, real-time tracking, and estimated fares of a trip. It has a dynamic rate-calculation model that is based on demand and supply which ensures availability all the time. However, some of the disadvantages include high peak rates for service provision as well as issues to do with fare satisfaction for drivers. Careem  operates as an app with ride hailing service, fare calculation and sharing service along with other services that include food and package delivery. It works according to geographical regions and has a reward program for the frequent users. However, it lacks adequate delivery service to customers in local areas and sometimes experiences glitches. Lyft  is centered on giving a pleasant driver and passenger experience and ride choices and encouraging shared rides for the environment. Indeed, it focuses on the driver’s feedback and electric vehicle using. However, it has limited global reach and higher costs in some regions which reduces its competitiveness. InDrive   have a very unique feature that passengers and drivers can freely set fares with one another, the company offers an adjustable price range. It also provides affordability since it eliminates standard fares charges. However, there are many problems such as inconsistency of price expectations and conflicts between users. Bykea  focuses majorly on motor bike ride hailing, parcel delivery services and mobile money products for working in populous cities. It relies on motorcycles for efficient and cheap services. Currently it is focused on bikes only and does not have options for car or auto-rickshaw transportation which significantly narrows down its range of customers. Bolt  has convenient services such as ride sharing, food delivery, scooter services all of which are cheap with emphasis on quick delivery. It advertises itself with real time tracking and competitive prices with the aim of attracting the users. However, being able to standardize service delivery across the various regions is still a major issue. Yango  offers first and last-mile transportation services that are cheap and include local payment options and the ability to monitor the ride in real time. It aims at achieving wider outreach and the modular design allows implementation in less developed areas and even in small cities. Yet, it does not possess highly developed riding algorithm matching that may have an impact on the consumer level. DiDi  has many services that are customized to serve the Asian and the Latin American population like ride hailing, bike sharing and food delivery. It applies data science and analytics for the pairing of riders to the nearest driver. But it comes across legal bottlenecks and issues concerning data privacy in some of the relevant markets. Grab  combines mobility, delivery, and fintech in one application. It adapts a localized strategy to achieve that. However, drawbacks include high cost and at times, the application slows down during certain periods in a day. Ola  offers various car categories for its clients, starting from auto rickshaw and ending with electric cars. It employs price discrimination and incentives to drivers to guarantee that a car is always available. However, it does not have a proper customer support service, and sometimes fails to provide enough drivers.

heading: Proposed Methodology and Architecture
content: This diagram (Figure 1) illustrates the architecture of the "GoMate", highlighting the interaction between its key components. The system is divided into four main parts: Users interact with modules like booking and tracking through the frontend, built using React Native; the backend using Python (Flask/Django) for authentication, ride matching, ride management, fare calculation and payment processing; database using PostgreSQL to store user data, ride details and payment records; and external integrations with Google Maps API for location services and Googlr OR-Tools for route optimization. The diagram shows how these components communicate through API calls, ensuring smooth operation of the app's features. Figure 1: Abstract architecture diagram

heading: Methodology
content: The development of the "GoMate" ride-sharing app follows a structured approach, ensuring smooth integration of key components to deliver an efficient and user-friendly experience. The system architecture as shown in figure 1 is organized into interconnected modules, each performing a specific function User Module: This module manages user registration, login, profile information, and access permissions. It connects to the User Data Storage to store and retrieve user information securely. Ride Booking Module: This module is responsible for receiving the user ride requests and facilitating ride booking by having the user select pickup and drop-off location. It acts as the entry point for users requesting rides and connects with the Location Module to get accurate coordinates for ride management. Location Module: The location module interacts with mapping services to get the coordinates for pickup and drop-off points. This module also determines the current location of users and drivers, feeding this data into both the Tracking & Notification Module and the Ride Sharing decision-making process. Ride Sharing Decision: This decision point determines whether a ride request can be shared with another user based on proximity and similar routes. If the criteria for ride-sharing is met, the Ride Matching Module is activated; otherwise, the Ride Management Module handles it as a single ride. Ride Matching Module: This module identifies potential ride matches for shared rides based on location, route, and timing constraints. The module works with the Route Optimization Module to determine the most efficient route for multiple pickups and drop-offs. Route Optimization Module: This module uses Google OR-Tools to calculate the optimal route to minimize travel time and cost for both shared and individual rides. Route optimization ensures efficient fuel usage and helps the driver avoid unnecessary detours to improve service quality. Ride Management Module: This module manages the overall process of each ride. It is also responsible for updating ride statuses and handling cancellations. It communicates with both the Tracking & Notification Module for real-time status updates and the Database to store ride information in Ride Data Storage. Tracking & Notification Module: This module provides real-time updates ride status, arrival time, and notifications for changes. It uses data from the Location Module to track the ride and keep both parties informed. Fare Calculation Module: The fare calculation module calculates the total cost of each ride based on distance, time, and ride-sharing options. This module takes input from the Route Optimization Module to accurately calculate the cost, which is displayed to the user before confirming the ride. Database (User Data Storage and Ride Data Storage): The database stores all user and ride data. User profiles and ride history are stored in User Data Storage and Ride Data Storage, respectively, ensuring data is available for ride management, history tracking, and future reference.

heading: Database Technologies
content: PostgreSQL: It is a robust relational database that's particularly well-suited for ride-sharing applications. Its PostGIS extension provides powerful geospatial capabilities for location-based queries, while its ACID compliance ensures data integrity during critical operations like ride matching. PostgreSQL's ability to handle concurrent users and complex queries makes it an excellent choice for scaling the application as it’s user base grows.

heading: Methodology:
content: The report formatter is developed with a structured pipeline to ensure that it is properly formatted and that the content of the reports is classified based on data AI to identify the essential elements of the report. The interconnecting modules constituting the architecture (Figure 1) are each with a unique purpose. 1. Admin Panel Module: This module defines formatting templates, such as margins, table styles, placement of captions, hierarchy of headings, font size, and style. The templates are stored in the Template Database. 2. User Module (Students): This module handles registration, logins and submission of reports by students. It provides file upload services of text, PDF, and word documents. 3. File Upload and Parsing Module: It receives uploaded files and removes their raw content (text, tables and figures) and converts the information into a structured format to enable AI to process it. 4. AI Content Classification Module: The NLP model marks the sections (Heading 1, Heading 2, paragraphs, tables, photos, captions, references, etc.) of the text. It provides the Formatting Engine with directed content. 5. Formatting Engine Module: It uses standards of the university template to a content that is categorized and controls captions, margins, spacing, numbering and styles of headers. A draft report is generated. 6. Other AI Services: Plagiarism and grammar checker ensure the accuracy and originality. AI recommendations provides recommendations to missing portions of the paper, including the Conclusion. 7. Table of Contents/ Numbering Module: This will automatically generate a list of figures, list of tables and table of contents. It perfectly places captions (under the pictures, on the top of the tables). 8. Collaboration & Version Control Module: It allows a number of different students to post and merge sections. The rollback version history is also maintained. 9. Live Preview Module: It provides a preview of the organized report live. Students can see changes immediately, as it works with Overleaf. 10. Image Ethics Detection Module: This recognizes ethical or unethical images uploaded and beforehand inserts them, based on pre-trained computer vision models (e.g. ResNet, CLIP or custom CNNs). The moraceous pictures pass, the immoral row. 11. Voice to Command Module: Speech recognition engine converts the spoken instructions into actions (e.g. bold heading, insert caption). It uses commands to format actions relying on ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition) and NLP intent-classification.

heading: ABSTRACT
content: Due to social media's widespread influence in modern society, there has been much discussion about how social media use affects health. This report offers a thorough analysis of the relationship between social media usage and various aspects of health. By synthesizing research findings and analysis, the study aims to clarify the intricate relationship between social media platforms and individual well-being. The study's goal is to identify the positive and negative effects of social media on health outcomes, including social, mental, and physical dimensions. The executive summary, which uses a qualitative approach, provides a nuanced perspective free of acronyms or jargon, making it easy to understand for readers with a wide range of backgrounds. Key findings indicate that while social media facilitates communication, connectivity, and access to health-related information, it also engenders challenges such as cyberbullying, addiction, and unrealistic social comparisons. The report also discusses the possible effects of social media on mental health disorders like anxiety, depression, and problems with self-esteem.

heading: INTRODUCTION
content: Social media has an undeniable impact on modern society, influencing all facets of interpersonal relationships and social structures. But amid its widespread use is a landscape full of complexities and implications that need careful examination. This introduction sets out to analyze the complex effects of social media with the goal of shedding light on these effects and offering understanding of their significant influence. Individual behaviors, cultural norms, and communication patterns have all undergone an unparalleled shift as a result of social media platforms' remarkable growth. Worries about how this change will affect people's mental health, relationships with others, consumer behavior, public opinion, economic dynamics, and cultural phenomena are also growing along with this change. In light of the consequences of a world growing more digitally interconnected, it is critical for society to comprehend and manage these complexities. The goals of this conversation are multiple: To examine social media's complex effects on modern society from a number of angles. To shed light on the opportunities and difficulties that come with social media in the digital age and promote a better comprehension of how it shapes social structures and human interactions. In order to grab readers' attention and emphasize the importance of more research into this developing phenomenon, the main conclusions and trends drawn from research, statistical data, and expert insights will be highlighted. To highlight the need of using thoughtful, nuanced methods and well-informed strategies to navigate the complexities of social media's impact on people and societies. In order to gather information for this discussion, a thorough evaluation of academic papers, empirical studies, statistical data, and professional opinions from reliable sources in the domains of technology, sociology, psychology, economics, and communication studies was conducted. In order to provide a comprehensive understanding of the subject matter, methodological approaches included systematic literature reviews, quantitative analysis of survey data, qualitative analysis of case studies, and synthesis of various perspectives. Upon careful analysis of the data and conclusions, a number of noteworthy revelations have surfaced: Use of social media is linked to higher rates of depression, anxiety, and low self-esteem, especially in younger populations. Social media improves communication and creates support systems, but it also creates problems like cyberbullying, flimsy relationships, and privacy issues. Social media's incorporation into business is changing how people behave, how they make decisions, and what new business opportunities it opens up. Social media has a significant impact on democracy and public opinion. It also has an impact on political polarization, echo chambers, and disinformation. Social media accelerates and globalizes cultural trends, resulting in the celebration of diversity as well as cultural homogenization.

Only the sender and receiver are able to see / access the content and read / listen to these messages. The service provider cannot even see the communication. End-to-end encryption reduces the likelihood of hacking or data breaches.  Sure Message Delivery:  Messages are not available or recognizable by third parties during their delivery.  Integrity and Authenticity: Verification of the message as coming from the intended recipient and that it has not been changed using digital signatures or cryptology.  User Trust and Privacy Protection: Sharing sensitive or personal information makes users feel secure, therefore increasing platform trust.  Characteristics for additional security:  Messages that self-destruct.  Multi-factor authentication.  Safe backup.  Block screen capture or sending of sensitive message threads.  Confidentiality: Only authorized users can access or view the messages.  Building Trust:  A reliable system encourages users to share their information without disclosing it.  Scalability: The platform is suitable for small teams in vast organizations. c) Feature List  End-to-end encrypted messaging.  Secure voice / video calling with encrypted stream.  Image sharing with built-in encryption.  Voice Messaging with encrypted audio recordings.  User authentication (passwords, multi-factor login).  Secure file transfer between users.  Role-based access control/Authorization.  Self-destructing messages with expiry timers.  Offline mode (queued messages offline & delivered securely with reconnected).  Cross-platform availability.  Simple, user-friendly interface. d) Objectives  To design and develop a trustable and secure communication platform  To ensure data protection using the principles of confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA)  To provide a safe and trustable medium for personal and organizational communication  To emphasize the use of latest cryptographic techniques in system  To make a foundation for reliable and trusted messaging  for future use.

heading: Refactoring
content: Latent semantic analysis a b s t r a c t The presence of code smells will increase the risk of failure, make software difficult to maintain, and introduce potential technique debt in the future. Although many deep-learning-based approaches have been proposed to detect code smells, most existing works suffer from the problem of incomplete feature extraction and unbalanced distribution between positive samples and negative samples. Furthermore, the accuracy of existing works can be further improved. This paper proposes a novel approach named DeleSmell to detect code smells based on a deep learning model. The dataset is built by extracting samples from 24 real-world projects. To improve the imbalance in the dataset, a refactoring tool is developed to automatically transform good source code into smelly code and to generate positive samples based on real cases. DeleSmell collects both structural features through iPlasma and semantic features via latent semantic analysis and word2vec. DeleSmell’s model includes a convolutional neural network(CNN) branch and gate recurrent unit(GRU)-attention branch. The final classification is conducted by an support vector machine(SVM). In the experimentation, the effectiveness of DeleSmell is evaluated by answering seven research questions. The experimental results show that DeleSmell improves the accuracy of brain class (BC) and brain method (BM) code smells detection by up to 4.41% compared with existing approaches, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. © 2022 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

heading: 1. Introduction
content: Code smells are not bugs of a program but poor implemen- tation choices that may signify the weakness of software design. Although it is a surface indication of code structure, code smells may expose a deeper problem in a software system. The presence of code smells may increase the risk of failure, make software difficult to maintain, and introduce potential technique debt in the future. Detecting code smells has become increasingly important for software evolution. More than 20 kinds of code smells have been identified in thousands of real-world projects. Palomba et al. [1] conducted a survey with 162 developers and discovered that more than 90% of developers focus on prevalent code smells (such as feature envy, god class, and long method) rather than seldom- used code smells, such as brain class (BC) and brain method (BM). BC/BM code smells usually have numerous structural branches and deeply recursive invocations, which disobeys the proportion rule and increases the risk of failure. ∗ Corresponding author. E-mail address: zhangyang@hebust.edu.cn (Y. Zhang). Many works have been conducted to identify code smells since the automated detection tool was originally proposed [2]. Traditional approaches employ heuristic-based approaches [3,4] by computing a collection of metrics. A predefined threshold is set to distinguish between smelly samples and nonsmelly sam- ples. However, code snippets with different behaviors may use the same metric and consequently have a totally different code smells. Furthermore, choosing a proper threshold requires ex- pertise. Lacking experience and holding potential bias have a negative impact on making the appropriate decision. Some re- searchers have improved code smells detection by employing machine learning (ML) techniques, such as K-means [5], sup- port vector machine (SVM) [6], and naive bayes [7]. However, these techniques suffer from insufficient feature extraction [8]. As a result, the accuracy of their results is not satisfactory. In recent years, some researchers have begun to detect code smells by leveraging deep learning techniques, including convolutional neural network(CNN) [9], long short-term memory(LSTM) [10], and residual network(ResNet) [11]. Most works initially build a dataset by extracting features from the source code and then train a deep learning model to obtain a classifier. Deep-learning-based approaches significantly improve the accuracy of code smell de- tection. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.knosys.2022.109737 0950-7051/© 2022 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. Y. Zhang, C. Ge, S. Hong et al. Knowledge-Based Systems 255 (2022) 109737 Although many works on code smell detection have been conducted, several problems remain open. First, existing approaches mainly focus on structural features of the source code, while semantic features are prone to being disregarded. Consequently, the features learned by the model may be biased. Second, existing works lack a unified dataset for different code smells. Additionally, the deep-learning-based model can be further optimized. Third, the existing data en- hancement algorithm synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) [12] is not visualized. Some samples generated by SMOTE probably disturb the boundary between positive samples and negative samples (illustrated in Section 3). To address these problems, this paper proposes a novel ap- proach named DeleSmell to detect code smells based on a deep learning model. To increase the number of positive samples, a refactoring tool is developed to automatically transform nons- melly items into smelly items in real-world projects. DeleSmell extracts both structural features by iPlasma [13] and semantic features by latent semantic analysis (LSA) [14] and word2vec [15]. Thus, a dataset with more than 200,000 samples is con- structed from 24 real-world projects. DeleSmell builds a deep neural network model, including a CNN branch and gate recurrent unit(GRU)-attention branch. The final classification is conducted by an SVM. In the experimentation, the effectiveness of De- leSmell is evaluated by answering seven research questions. The experimental results show that DeleSmell improves the accu- racy of BC/BM code smells detection by up to 4.41% compared with existing approaches, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: • A novel approach named DeleSmell is proposed to detect code smells based on the deep learning model and LSA. • A refactoring tool is developed to automatically generate positive samples of the dataset. • A dataset with more than 200,000 samples is built from 24 real-world projects. • Many experiments have been conducted to evaluate the ef- fectiveness of DeleSmell by answering seven research ques- tions. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2 examines related works. Section 3 illustrates the motivation of our work. Section 4 presents an overview of DeleSmell and the design of each component. The experimental setup and results are reported in Section 5. This paper is concluded in Section 6.

heading: 2. Related works
content: In recent years, many works on code smell detection by heuristic-based, ML-based, and deep-learning-based approaches have been conducted [16–20]. In this section, we present the background on code smell detection and elaborate on the related literature.

heading: 2.1. Heuristic based detection
content: The heuristic-based approach identifies the symptoms of a code smell and then chooses a set of thresholds for some met- rics to detect code smells. Tsantalis et al. [21] presented a tool JDeodorant to detect code smells. The empirical evaluation of the performance of this tool demonstrates an average improvement in accuracy of 75%. Marinescu et al. [13] proposed a detection tool iPlasma to detect code problems such as identity disharmonies, collaboration disharmonies and classification disharmonies. iPlasma is an integrated platform for evaluating the quality of object-oriented software from several aspects, such as model extraction and high-level metric analysis. The detection tool DECOR [3] defined a set of approaches for automatic design and code smell detection (also known as Anti-Pattern). DECOR combines metrics with thresholds and extracts the features af- fected by code smell. This detection tool identifies code smell and automatically generates the detection algorithms by templates. However, since different tools have different rules for detecting code smell, it is possible that different results can be obtained for the same code.

heading: 2.2. Machine-learning-based detection
content: Some researchers have leveraged machine-learning-based techniques for code smell detection. Machine learning techniques utilize a supervised learning approach to analyze a sufficiently large number of samples and train them. In contrast to heuristics, this approach relies on classifiers to distinguish whether the source code is smelly, rather than defining thresholds based on computational metrics. Amorim et al. [22] presented an em- pirical report that evaluates the use of a decision tree classi- fication algorithm to identify code smells in different projects. Fontana et al. [23] applied several machine learning models and compared the performance of these models by considering four performance metrics. Guggulothu et al. [5] employed multilabel classification to detect whether a given code element is affected by multiple code smells. Alazba et al. [24] proposed an inte- grated learning approach to detect code smells. The output of an ML classifier is combined and then re-output. The results are predicted after fitting the output of all the basic classifiers. The experimental results show that the accuracy of integrated learning is higher than that of a single ML classifier.

heading: 2.3. Deep-learning-based detection
content: To learn the deeper features, researchers have started to use deep learning models for code smell detection. Ananta et al. [9] employed a one-dimensional convolutional neural network to detect BC/BM and obtained 97% accuracy and 94% accuracy, respectively. Palomba et al. [1] proposed a code smell inten- sity prediction model that relies on both technical aspects and community-related aspects. Liu et al. [25] proposed an auto- matic approach to generating labeled training data for the neural network-based classifier, which does not require any human intervention. Sharma et al. [10] applied deep learning models in detecting code smells without carrying out extensive feature engineering and compared the performance of different mod- els. Their exploration not only shows the feasibility of applying transfer learning for identifying code smells but also compares the performance of deep learning models in the transfer learning context.

heading: 3. Motivation
content: This section presents the motivation to demonstrate the ra- tionale. Building the dataset is important for deep-learning-based detection. During this procedure, it is important to maintain the balance between positive samples and negative samples. Pecorelli et al. [26] empirically compared five techniques of code smell de- tection and suggested that SMOTE obtained the best performance. MARS [11] is a detection approach for BC/BM code smells and balances the dataset by leveraging SMOTE. However, this data enhancement approach suffers from several problems. SMOTE randomly selects minorities as candidates to automatically gen- erate similar samples. Not all samples are suitable to be selected for expansion. According to the principle of SMOTE, we illustrate a

Y. Zhang, C. Ge, S. Hong et al. Knowledge-Based Systems 255 (2022) 109737 Fig. 1. Data enhancement of SMOTE. possible situation in Fig. 1. The blue dots and green dots represent positive samples and negative samples, respectively. The orange dots located near the boundary represent the seeds chosen by SMOTE. The new samples generated by SMOTE probably become closer to the boundary, as shown in Fig. 1(b). As a result, the boundary between positive samples and negative samples may become disturbed, resulting in incorrect classification results. Existing approaches [11,27] rely on structural features of source codes, while semantic features are prone to being disre- garded. The difference between semantic analysis and structural analysis lies in the procedure of feature extraction. The semantic features leverage text mining algorithms to calculate the text similarity. Palomba et al. [27] utilized structural and semantic analysis to obtain version information of several Java projects. The results highlight that code smell detected through semantic analysis are generally perceived as dangerous as code smells de- tected through structural features, even if they do not exceed any structural metrics’ thresholds. Additionally, the results emphasize that the structural and semantic information are complementary; however, few works have been conducted to combine this in- formation. Furthermore, most semantic analysis approaches only consider identifiers and comments and do not analyze semantic features of the source code. This approach is limited if the iden- tifier or method is not named according to its function or if the comment is not relevant to the method.

Both semantic and struc- tural features are extracted from these projects. To obtain the semantic features of the source code, we generate the word vec- tors by word2vec and calculate the average conceptual similarity (ACSM) by LSA. Structural features are extracted by employing code metrics such as coupling between two object classes (CBO), access to foreign data (ATFD), lines of code (LOC), etc., based on iPlasma [13]. heading: 4.1. Data collection
content: We generate the dataset by taking a two-pronged approach for data collection. First, we conduct a breadth-oriented study by collecting 24 real-world projects from GitHub.1 Seventeen of

heading: 1 https://github.com/
content: 24 projects contain more than 5,000 number of methods (NOM). Furthermore, the LOC of most projects is substantially greater than 30,000. Table 1 presents projects and their configurations. Second, we conduct a depth-oriented study on the features of the source code by semantic and structural analysis, which will be illustrated in Section 4.3.

heading: 4.2. Automatic items generation
content: To prevent underfitting, we need numerous samples to im- prove the generalization of the neural network. However, the number of code smells in existing open-source projects is not enough to support the training of neural networks, which results in an imbalanced the dataset. To solve this problem, we generate smelly code by refactoring. Different from existing refactoring applied to smelly software to improve software quality, our refac- toring is applied to well-designed programs to generate code smells. We develop a refactoring tool to convert a normal method into a BM. This method can generate numerous labeled training sam- ples for deep-learning-based detection. A method is considered to be a BM if an increasing number of functions are added to this method until it becomes out of control [28]. If we merge multiple methods into one method, the integrated method has multiple roles and thus can be considered a BM. DeleSmell employs the rules [9] to label the items. This tool automatically generates items without any human intervention. Thus, we can obtain a large number of labeled items from all kinds of projects. An overview of the refactoring framework is shown in Fig. 3. The tool begins by automatically abstracting the source code into an abstract syntax tree (AST) and by generating a call graph. The tool walks through the AST to locate a method m that could be a positive item through refactoring. m is selected by the following rules: (a) the cyclomatic complexity (CYCLO) of m satisfies Eq. (1), where Cm represents the CYCLO of method m and N represents the number of methods in a project. (b) m is not polymorphic. If several methods overwrite in children class m, it cannot be in- lined [29]. The call graph is then analyzed to obtain the invocation of the selected method m. We develop the refactoring tool under the Eclipse JDT framework and use these analyses and rules to ensure that the refactoring will correctly generate positive items.

heading: 4.3.2. Structural features extraction
content: Multiple metrics are selected to detect a kind of code smell since each metric has a different role and weight. We employ iPlasma [13] to extract structural metrics from the method or the class in a specific project. In addition to the metrics of a method, we also use the metrics of project, package, and class. We select 24 metrics for BC code smell and 21 metrics for BM code smell. The chosen metrics are presented in Table 4. These metrics (such as average methods weight (AMW), FANIN, FANOUT, etc.) are commonly employed in the field of code smell detection.

heading: 4.3.3. Features integration
content: The vector extracted from each item is taken as a sample of the dataset. The format of a vector is defined in Eq. (6). < m1, m2, . . . ,mn, s1, s2, s3, ACSM > (6) where mi represents the ith metrics, n represents the number of selected code metrics, sj denotes the jth word vector extracted from the source code by word2vec, and ACSM represents the average conceptual similarity. The BM dataset has more than 200,000 samples, while the BC dataset contains more than 22,000 samples. The final dataset contains approximately 38% positive samples.

heading: 4.4. Deep learning model
content: The model is critical to improving the performance of code smell detection. Inspired by Jiang’s work [35], we propose a model with a CNN and GRU-attention in parallel and leverage an SVM as the classifier. Fig. 5 presents the architectural overview of our model. The input is processed by a GRU-attention branch and CNN branch in parallel. The CNN branch consists of a feature extraction compo- nent followed by a classification component. The feature extrac- tion component is composed of a set of hidden layers, including convolution, batch normalization, and dropout layers. The out- put of the last dropout layer is connected to the input of a densely connected network that consists of a stack of two dense layers. The reason why we employ a GRU is that it can save a considerable amount of time in the presence of numerous training samples. An attention mechanism is introduced in the GRU branch to learn the important features in the dataset while suppressing the interference of irrelevant information on the clas- sification results. For an SVM, the kernel method can be utilized Fig. 5. Deep learning model of DeleSmell. to map the nonlinear samples to high dimensional space and to identify the optimal hyperplane by maximizing the classifica- tion interval between two samples. The input of the last dense layer consists of the features concatenated by the GRU-attention branch and CNN branch and is connected to an SVM for the final classification. We tune the hyperparameters of the classifier by applying the grid search algorithm [36]. To avoid overfitting of the neural network, we employ certain optimization techniques. First, the function ReLU is selected as the activation function instead of the function Sigmoid in the convolution layers. Second, we penalize the loss function through L2 regularization at the dense layer. Generally, L2 regularization is better than L1 regularization if there is no particular concern for certain explicit features. Last, we use dropout layers with a ratio of 0.3. Additionally, we leverage Adam to optimize the defined model. The function fit() is used to train the model; its parameters include the data, labels, number of epochs, validation_data, and batch size. During the model training procedure, we set the epochs to 80 and the batch size to 16.

heading: 5. Evaluation
content: This section introduces the experimental setup and then presents the research questions and evaluation metrics. The ex- perimental results are illustrated. For the reproducibility of the evaluation, all models and datasets are available at https://uzhan gyang.github.io/research/delesmell.html.

heading: 5.1. Setup
content: All experiments are conducted on a workstation with a 2.6 GHz Intel Core i7 CPU and 16 GB main memory running 64-bit Win- dows 10. The Python version is 3.6, the TensorFlow version is 2.4.1 and the Keras version is 2.4.3. Table 5 presents the configurations of all models.

heading: 5.2. Research questions
content: We evaluate the effectiveness of DeleSmell by answering the following research questions (RQ): RQ1 Is DeleSmell more effective than ML-based approaches? RQ2 Is our model more applicable than existing deep learning models for code smell detection? RQ3 How effective is DeleSmell in detecting BC/BM code smell compared with previous works?

heading: ABSTRACT
content: Skin health is an essential aspect of overall well-being, yet many individuals struggle to access personalized skincare guidance. Existing skincare applications are often limited to brand-driven product marketing or provide generic solutions that fails to address diverse skin tones, local environment factors, and individual lifestyles. To overcome these limitations, this project proposes SkinIQ- an AI-powered skincare assistant. The system will analyze user skin images using computer vision models, provide quiz-based assessments for users unable to upload photos, and recommend skincare products filtered by ingredients, budget, and local availability. Furthermore, the system will integrate holistic lifestyle advice including diet, hydration, and sleep, while enabling progress tracking and community interaction. By combining artificial intelligence, dermatological insights, and contextual awareness (e.g., climate, allergies), SkinIQ aims to deliver a personalized, safe, and accessible skincare experience. The expected outcome is a functional web-based platform that empowers users to understand, manage, and improve their skin health effectively.

heading: Domain background
content: The global skincare industry has rapidly expanded in the last decade, with consumers increasingly seeking personalized skincare recommendations. Conventional dermatological consultations can be costly and inaccessible, particularly in developing regions. Mobile applications such as Skinive, HelloAva, and Haut. AI have attempted to address this gap using AI-based skin analysis. However, these platform primarily focus on marketing specific brands, lack inclusivity for diverse skin tones, and often ignore local product availability and lifestyle factors. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Computer Vision have shown strong potential in healthcare applications, especially in areas like dermatology where image-based analysis can detect skin issues such as acne, scars, pigmentation, or dryness, At the same time, integrating lifestyle and environmental context is essential since skincare is not limited to topical treatments also influenced by diet, hydration, and climate conditions.

heading: Motivation and Significance of the Project
content: Most existing skincare platforms fail to provide holistic, locally relevant solutions, creating a disparity in access to quality advice for users globally, particularly in Low-and Middle-Income Countries. These platforms often rely on expensive international product recommendations and suffer from AI bias and underrepresentation regarding diverse skin tones, with models performing poorly on varied datasets. This critical gap is compounded by the neglect of essential holistic factors like diet, sleep, and local climate in their recommendations. SkinIQ is proposed to overcome these ethical and practical failings by building a comprehensive, affordable, and inclusive AI-based assistant. We are motivated to tune our AI models for skin tones, integrate non-visual data like lifestyle and local product availability (PKR-based), and ultimately deliver personalized, accessible skincare guidance that closes the gap left by existing, limited approaches.

heading: Proposed Solution
content: To address these issues, this project proposes SkinIQ- an AI-powered web application that integrates: AI-based skin image analysis to detect common conditions such as acne, dryness, or scars. Interactive skin quiz assessments for inclusivity. Personalized product recommendations with filters for budget, allergens, and local availability. Holistic advice including diet, hydration, sleep, and seasonal skincare routines. Progress tracking via before/after comparisons and habit reminders. Community interaction and education to build user engagement and trust. By combining these features, SkinIQ will offer a unique, localized, and user- centric platform.

heading: Expected Outcomes
content: The expected deliverables include: A functional AI-powered web application. A product recommendation system integrated with a local skincare product database (PKR-based) A lifestyle advisory module providing hydration, sleep, and seasonal advice. Progress tracking features with image uploads and graphical reports. A scalable architecture enabling future integration with dermatologists for severe cases.

heading: Problem Statement
content: Most existing skincare platforms are limited, offering generic or brand-driven solutions that fail to address the complexities of individual skin health, particularly for diverse skin tones and local environments. They rely heavily on costly international product recommendations, ignoring local availability and budget constraints, and often focus narrowly on visual analysis without integrating essential holistic factors like diet, sleep, and climate. This gap highlights the need for a comprehensive, affordable, and inclusive AI-based assistant that provides actionable, localized insights and personalized recommendations tailored to a user’s full lifestyle and context.

heading: Project Objective
content: The main focused objectives for the SkinIQ project are: To develop an AI-powered web applications for the holistic diagnosis and management of common skin conditions. To integrate AI-based skin image analysis and an inclusive, detailed skin quiz for condition detection. To implement a personalized product recommendation system filtered by budget, local availability (PKR-based), and ingredient safety. To incorporate a holistic advisory module for diet, hydration, sleep, and seasonal/weather- based skincare routines. To validate the system’s accuracy and usability against success criteria with a target of at least 70% user satisfaction.

heading: Related Work
content: Several AI-driven skincare solutions exist in the market, but they have limitations:

heading: Bias and Underrepresentation in Skin Tone
content: A paper titled “Disparities in dermatology AI performance on a diverse, curated clinical image set” (DDI dataset) shows that many state-of-the-art AI dermatology models perform substantially worse on dark skin tones and uncommon diseases. The drop in ROC-AUC is large when models trained on lighter skin/homogenous data are tested on more diverse datasets. Another recent study “Beyond Accuracy: A Cost-Aware Approach to Skin Lesion Detection Across Skin Tone Imbalances” emphasizes that datasets such as Fitzpatrick 17k are heavily imbalanced toward lighter skin tones. Models tend to bias toward those, and performance suffers on darker skin unless explicitly addressed.

heading: Limited Contextual / Environmental / Lifestyle Factors
content: A study “Skin health response to climate change weather tailored cosmetics using artificial intelligence” (Lee, JMAI) reviews how climate, weather, UV, temperature, etc., affect skin, but notes that although this line of research is promising, evidence is limited. The study particularly says there is a gap in linking environmental/lifestyle/habit data with product recommendations in AI systems. Many AI skincare tools focus mainly on analyzing images (blemishes, fine lines, pigmentation, moisture) or matching ingredients, but less on diet, lifestyle, variation by climate or local pollution, etc. For example “Deep learning-based skin care product recommendation: A focus on cosmetic ingredient analysis and facial skin conditions” integrates ingredient analysis and skin concerns but still relies mostly on facial image + product ingredient data; lifestyle or climate context are less present.

heading: Local and Market-Relevance Issues
content: The systematic review “Diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence for dermatological conditions: a systematic review focused on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs)” shows that many studies are from high-income settings, and LMICs face issues like resource limitations, underrepresented skin types, and data access constraints. This often means recommendations or product availability in AI systems are mismatched to LMIC realities. Also, underrepresentation in datasets (for skin of color) arises not just in images but in metadata: many works fail to record or use skin tone, lighting conditions, etc., making it hard to adapt models to varied local contexts.
