heading: Introduction
content: Higher education has become one of the essential elements in  modeling individual occupational paths, socio-economic growth and international standing. World university ranking system has become a crucial mechanism for students, researchers, policymakers, and educational establishments as nowadays, globally universities are appraised on behalf of their academic reputation, research environment, staff competency, student faculty ratio, international outlook etc. World's well known university ranking Systems such as QS, THE, ARWU has provided uniform criteria that affects the organizational reputation and decision making of an individual. These systems have significant influence on Potential learners  identenfying their right choice of instituation, researchers exploring alliances and  government formulating academic policies. Existing global ranking systems , regardless of their significance, uses a one-size-fits-all methodology that focuses on standardized benchmark overlooking the needs of varirty of users. As is well known, QS focuses on academic and employer reputation, faculty/student ratio, citation per faculty and international faculty and student ratio, however, THE gives weight to teaching quality, research environment and quality, industry impact and international outlook. In the same way, ARWU prioritizes nobles award winners and highly citied researchers, publications and per capita performance. These indicators yield informative outcomes yet they they might overlook the preferences that academics and individual students finds important. A student focusing on career development prioritizes employer reputation, however, a student focusing on scholary work gives more weight reasech environment and quality. In this way, customized preferences are neglected and stakeholders are left with one uniform ranking result that unable to reflect the needs of variety of users having diverse priorities. The motivation for this project appears from the natural limitation of fixed ranking systems and the need for a personalized one. Global rankings effects academic and professional choices yearly, yet they fail to feed to multiple individual choices . For example, a student following research may focus on faculty skillfulness and publication impact, whereas another focused on capability may value alumni success and employer recognition more. This requires the need for flexible judging tools . Moreover, fast AI development has made it possible to analyze user behaviours and preferences which helps to generate data-driven personalized recommendation. Using Ai for adaptive university ranking can transform how students , researchers and policy-makers make higher education planning. This project is important because it fulfiils user needs and wants making ranking more personal and meaningful. It keeps the trust and accuracy of existing systems but adds a human touch, something that helps people make choices and that actually fit their own needs and preferences. The basic purpose of this project is to compose and create a Personalized University Ranking and Recommendation Platform that allows users to create custom-made university rankings and receive AI-driven suggestions. The aim of the system is to: Analyze ranking data from QS, THE, and ARWU without mixing their methodologies; Enable users to assign custom weights to factors such as research, faculty-student ratio, and employability; and Provide AI-based university recommendations adapted to user profiles and preferences. The scope of this project includes developing a multi-platform application (web and mobile), putting into practice a recommendation engine using AI techniques, and offering envisaged outputs to aid decision-making. However, the project does not aim to modify or merge the original ranking methodologies of QS, THE, or ARWU. Instead, it focuses completely on analyzing and deciphering their data to enhance user understanding and personalized capability. This project aims at the implementation of a Personalized University Ranking and Recommendation platform that uses datasets from leading ranking providers QS, THE and ARWU, while maintaining their methodologies discretely. Rather than combining criteria across datasets, the system will allow users to select a ranking dataset of their choice, and then customize results based on what parameters are available and assign weights to them within that dataset. In addition to basic customization, the system will also incorporate an AI-based recommendation engine that will learn user profiles, expressed preferences and implicit behavior to recommend universities that are a cultural and financial match for the user's academic, financial or professional goals. This blend of custom weighting and AI-powered recommendations will result in a hybrid solution that combines transparency with intelligent personalization. The indented result will be a functional cross-platform application designed to deliever personalized ranking result along with an integrated AI- based recommendation engine. User will have the ability to: Select from the different ranking providers while preserving the authenticity of evaluation methodology. Modify weigthing parameter within the dataset chosen according to user-specific choices Gain access to AI-powered recommendations that analyze both direct and indirect user needs. Seek to develop ranking results that will corresponds more closely with academic, financial or career objectives. View reports and charts that clearly show how preferences and AI suggestions affects the results. This project seeks to develop  a clear, dynamic, and user-centered platform that meaningfully strenghtens decision-making in academic planning, by preserving the reliability of existing ranking systems while integrating both a customization layer and an AI-driven recommendation module.

heading: Problem Statement:
content: Lack of personalization in current global university ranking systems like QS, THE, and ARWU results in a large gap between standardized metrics of evaluation and diverse individual user preferences. The systems provide consistent results that do not consider disparate priorities like research quality, affordability, teaching excellence, or employability. Consequently, learners and scholars can rarely determine most suitable institutions in accordance with their objectives, resulting in less-than-optimal academic and professional choices. Existing approaches are based on inflexible, one-size-fits-all weighting systems and do not utilize adaptive intelligence capable of inspecting user action or preferences. This shortcoming makes the provision of an intelligent, user-responsive system imperative with both existing rankings' credibility and added flexibility, and AI-powered personalization. Solving this issue will make decision-making in higher education stronger and offer a more meaningful and transparent evaluation framework.

heading: Project Objectives
content: The main goal of this project is to design and develop an AI-based web and mobile platform that provides personalized university ranking insights by analyzing global ranking systems such as QS, THE, and ARWU according to user-defined preferences. The following specific objectives have been defined to achieve this goal: To analyze and extract key parameters from major global university ranking datasets (QS, THE, ARWU) for comprehensive comparison and evaluation. To develop a unified analytical framework that interprets ranking parameters according to user priorities using normalization and weighting techniques. To build an AI-powered recommendation system that dynamically suggests universities best aligned with individual academic, financial, and regional preferences. To design and implement an interactive user interface for web and mobile platforms using React.js and React Native for seamless accessibility. To integrate a real-time database (Supabase) for managing user profiles, search history, and preference data securely. To enable push notifications and updates using Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) for user engagement and ranking insights. To monetize the platform through Google AdSense (web) and AdMob (mobile) while maintaining an ad-friendly user experience. To evaluate system performance and user satisfaction through testing, feedback, and measurable accuracy of AI-based recommendations.

heading: Related work
content: University ranking systems have a big impact on student decision-making and institutional reputation, they have been the focus of research and discussion for many years. Early attempts at ranking universities date back to the 1980s when the U.S. News & World Report introduced its college ranking system in the United States, primarily based on reputation surveys and statistical indicators . Since then, global ranking systems such as the QS World University Rankings, Times Higher Education (THE), and the Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU) have become the most significatn sources of institutional comparison. These rankings have shaped higher education by providing standardized indicators of performance, but their methodologies remain subject to criticism for lack of transparency and adaptability. QS World University Rankings:QS ranking system is based on the six parameters: academic reputation, employer reputation, faculty/student ratio, citations per faculty, international faculty ratio, and international student ratio . Focus on academic reputation, derived from surveys of academics worldwide, has made QS rankings highly significant in shaping perceptions of quality. However, critics argue that the reliance on survey-based data introduces subjectivity and potential bias, particularly against lesser-known institutions in developing regions .More, QS does not allow users to adjust the weight of these parameters, makes the system rigid for students with different preferences. Times Higher Education (THE) Rankings:THE ranking system focuses on 13 performance indicators grouped into five categories: teaching, research, citations, international outlook, and industry income . Unlike QS, THE covers a broader set of parameters that captures the  both academic and non-academic aspects of  the universities. Although THE takes a comprehensive approach, THE’s weighting system is fixed, meaning that teaching and research indicators may overshadow criteria that are more relevant to specific user groups, such as internationalization or employability . Studies suggest that despite providing insightful information, THE is still unavailable to users who want to customize ranking outputs according to their  personal goals . Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU): ARWU, developed by Shanghai Jiao Tong University, highlights research superiority by measuring Nobel Prize achievements, highly cited researchers, and publications in top journals . While ARWU is recognized for its impartiality, its heavy dependency on research indicators makes it less applicable for students essentially concerned with teaching quality, affordability, or employability. The system, like QS and THE, does not support customer-centeric personalization of ranking results. Research shows that ARWU’s methodology favors established institutions in developed countries, thus limiting its usefulness for students in other contexts . Criticism of Existing Rankings Scholars have censured global rankings for promoting a consistent and highly competitive model of higher education that often miss local contexts and individual user needs . Marginson  argues that global rankings strengthen reputational hierarchies rather than providing applicable perception for varying stakeholders. Additionally, Hazelkorn  highlights that uniform ranking models can entice students by highlighting reputation over practical ruminations such as financial cost, teaching quality, or alignment with personal academic goals.

heading: Success Criterion
content: The success of this project will be determined by its ability to provide a reliable, transparent, and user-friendly system that enhances traditional university rankings with personalization and AI-driven recommendations. The following measurable benchmarks will define project success: Dataset Utilization – The system must support the three major ranking providers (QS, THE, ARWU) individually, preserving their methodologies while allowing users to explore and customize results. Customizable Ranking within Each Dataset – Users must be able to adjust the weightage of parameters within a chosen ranking dataset (e.g., QS: employer reputation, faculty/student ratio; THE: teaching quality, citations; ARWU: research impact) and receive updated results that reflect their unique priorities. AI Recommendation System – The AI module must analyze user inputs, stated preferences, and interaction patterns to recommend a list of suitable universities, complementing the personalized ranking results. Cross-Platform Application – The system must function smoothly as a cross-platform application with an interactive and intuitive interface, ensuring accessibility on both desktop and mobile devices. Performance and Usability – The system should generate personalized ranking outputs and AI-based recommendations within an acceptable response time (e.g., less than 3 seconds for a query) and achieve at least 80% positive feedback in a usability test with sample users. Validation of Outcomes – The personalized rankings and AI recommendations must be validated against sample case studies (e.g., a student prioritizing affordability vs. a student prioritizing research) to confirm that results match expectations and enhance decision-making. By meeting these criteria, the project will achieve its primary goal: enabling users to extract maximum value from existing ranking systems while addressing their individual academic, financial, and career needs.

heading: ABSTRACT
content: Pakistan's economy depends heavily on agriculture, however rural farmers do not have access to many advantages, such as weather information, current expertise, and scientific farming practices. Traditional methods alongside literacy issues and poor connectivity hinder farmers from applying innovative solutions, and hence they face low returns and economic losses. The biggest problem is that farmers usually do not receive timely information regarding government schemes, correct crop calendars, and scientific information regarding soil and irrigation. Additionally, illiteracy limits their access to text-based programs, and in remote locations, unreliable internet makes online-only solutions unfeasible. To overcome these challenges, this project puts forth PakFasal, a Flutter-based mobile application that offers localized learning content, voice-to-text communication for uneducated farmers, offline data storage, and an immediate marketplace to bridge farmers with businesses. The app also incorporates weather prediction and IoT-based soil sensors (pH level and moisture) to provide real-time field information. Some of the expected outcomes are better decision-making in crop management, maximized water use and fertilizers, lowered reliance on intermediaries, and increased farmer participation. By combining mobile technology, voice interfaces, and IoT sensors, the app aims to empower farmers with knowledge and tools that increase productivity and support sustainable agriculture.

heading: Domain Background
content:
Agriculture forms the core of Pakistan's economy and provides employment to almost half of the labour force and adds considerably to GDP. Though critical to economic growth, the sector suffers from many challenges, especially in the rural sector, as farmers do not have easy access to information and technologies of modern farming methods. Farmers continue to use traditional farming methods handed down through generations, without scientific proof in many cases. This leads to low yield from crops, poor quality of farm products, and ineffective utilization of water and fertilizers. Modern farm methods, when utilized appropriately, are capable of raising productivity considerably, but there is a significant hurdle in the way of such knowledge becoming available in localized forms and versions so as to be understandable to farmers.

All the latest developments in the sector of Information and Communication Technology (ICT), especially mobile applications, have brought forth new ways to enhance agriculture-related activities. Even rural communities are now familiar with smartphones, and their potential needs to be utilized to present educational information, weather information, and direct marketing links. Apart from that, integration with Internet of Things (IoT) devices like moisture and pH sensors of the soil provides farmers with information in real time about their fields, enabling data-based decision-making. If localized voice-based support is also integrated with such networks for non-literate farmers, these networks have the capability to revolutionize the way knowledge of agriculture is distributed and practiced. Furthermore, the application of machine learning and decision support systems also makes agriculture smart. Machine learning applications can draw very precise predictions and customized suggestions by verifying huge databases of up-to-date and past data (such as weather, crops performance, soil health, and prices at the markets). The DSS can apply this data and assist producers in making critical decisions regarding which crops to grow, and at what time and frequency to plant and irrigate them, and how they can combat pests and diseases. When combined with local language assistance and vocal support for illiterate farmers, such technologies can transform conventional farming into smart, sustainable, and lucrative farming, bridging long-existing gaps between information sharing and resource use.

heading: Problem Statement
content: The three key challenges faced by Pakistan's farmers are: (1) inability to get timely localized agriculture information, such as government programs, crop calendars, and disease management strategies, (2) literacy and connectivity issues since most farmers are illiterate or semi-literate and inhabit regions with weak internet connectivity, and (3) reliance on unscientific agriculture practices, wherein irrigation and use of fertilizers are done on a guesswork basis without any scientific inputs. There are currently existing mobile applications and SMS platforms that have tried to solve some of these problems, but none of these solutions have offline capabilities, real-time weather forecasting, or connectivity with low-cost IoT devices. In view of, a complete, focused on farmers solution is urgently needed. Farmers in Pakistan lack localized information, are illiterate, have connectivity issues, and have no access to intelligent, mostly offline, sensors (IoT) based decision support system DSS.

heading: Proposed Solution
content: To address these problems, this project proposes PAKFASAL, a mobile application developed in Flutter that provides agricultural education and decision support in a farmer-centric manner. The app will deliver tutorials, articles, and videos in multiple local languages, ensuring accessibility for farmers across Pakistan. A voice-to-text interface will allow illiterate farmers to interact with the app naturally, while offline caching will make content available even in low-connectivity regions. The system integrates real-time weather forecasting and IoT-based soil sensors (pH and moisture), offering actionable insights on irrigation scheduling and fertilizer usage. In addition, the app will feature a farmer–company marketplace to eliminate middlemen and a query portal where farmers can upload crop issues (text, voice, or pictures) for expert or AI-driven responses. heading: Results or Outcomes
content: The social and economic outputs of PAKFASAL are anticipated. Farmers will have access to the correct, localized, and timely agricultural information, facilitating increased productivity and the quality of crops. Live weather and soil sensor integration will encourage scientific farming techniques, conserve water and enhancing soil health. The marketplace function will empower farmers by enabling them to buy inputs directly from firms at reduced costs and without the exploitative intermediaries. The addition of offline capabilities and voice functionality provides accessibility to illiterate and far-flung farmers. In sum, the system is designed to enhance agricultural production, lower expenses, and empower the farmer with information and technology, promoting sustainable agriculture and better livelihood.

heading: Problem Statement
content: Farmers in Pakistan face a range of interrelated hurdles that highly impede agricultural productivity and sustainability. The first hurdle relates to the relatively timely and localized agricultural information informing such as government support programs, crop calendars, and disease/pest management practices. Farmers therefore cannot make informed choices without such information sources. The second hurdle relates to the many illiteracy and connectivity challenges. Many farmers are illiterate or semi-illiterate and live in rural locations where connectivity is the most inadequate. This blocks those individuals from using digital tools or accessing newer knowledge of practices and innovations. Additionally, many farmers remain committed to using traditional or un-scientific practices and often make decisions around irrigation, fertilizer and pest management from instinct instead of from supporting data or information. While some mobile apps or SMS applications exist to challenge some of these issues, little exists to provide offline tools or real-time weather forecasts or connect with cost-sensitive IoT devices. In this context, we need to produce a solution that is holistic, farmer-centred and that could be used, even in low-connectivity situations, to build on intelligent decision support systems (DSS) based on sensors.

heading: Project Objectives
content: The overall goal of the PAKFASAL project is the creation of an intelligent farm platform that will supply location-based precise recommendations to the farmer with an integrated Suggestion System and Decision Support System (DSS).The platform is designed to support famers at making decisions on which crops to use, time of planting, irrigation scheduling, and disease management by processing real-time information on current weather and soil conditions and local farming practices. PAKFASAL distinguishes itself from other static sources of information by creating customized and personalized recommendations that address specific locations and requirements of each farmer, helping them be highly productive and take minimal risks. By its decision support functionality, the system enables famers to embrace sustainability, optimize use of sources, and overall increase efficiency in farm operations, which leads directly to enhanced crop output and agricultural development within Pakistan.

heading: Related work
content: In the last few years, there has been an interest in using Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) in agriculture to assist farmers in decision-making and management of resources. Some mobile applications and IoT solutions have been created globally, but most of them have not been localized, supported offline, or made accessible for illiterate farmers. One major category of related work is mobile-based agricultural advisory systems.

heading: mKrishi Platform:
content: The mKrishi platform in India provides location-specific advice to farmers via mobile phones [1]. Although it has enhanced farmer knowledge, its SMS dependence restricts its applicability for illiterate farmers.

heading: Digital Green Program:
content: The Digital Green program utilizes community videos to educate farmers but relies mostly on facilitators for implementation [2]. These systems show the potential of digital tools in agriculture but fail to offer interactive and self-service solutions.

heading: IoT-Based Smart Farming System:
content: Another area of research is IoT-based smart farming. Studies have shown the effectiveness of soil moisture and pH sensors for irrigation and fertilizer management. For instance, Jain et al. [3] recommended an IoT-based system that senses soil condition and sends data to the central server for data analysis. Such systems enhance efficiency in the use of resources but prove too expensive or complicated for small farmers in developing nations. The inclusion of affordable sensors on an easy-to-use mobile platform continues to be a gap in this technology.

heading: Weather forecasting Integration:
content: Weather forecasting integration is also becoming increasingly significant in precision agriculture. As per Mittal [4], the availability of weather information in a timely manner can play a major role in sowing and harvesting decisions, minimizing crop failure risks. However, most weather programs are designed for the public rather than farmers. Results can be improved by bridging this gap by combining agricultural recommendations with predictions.

heading: Voice-Based and Multilingual Interfaces:
content: Voice-based and multilingual interfaces have also been tested to make technology accessible to illiterate farmers. A study by Rahman et al. [5] proved that natural language interfaces enable illiterate users to interact well with mobile apps. However, few Agri-apps have employed this method, particularly in South Asian languages. In contrast to these current solutions, PAKFASAL is a one-stop-shop platform by integrating localized educational materials, offline usability, voice-to-text functionality, live weather forecasting, and IoT sensor integration within a single mobile app. This integrated approach not only overcomes technological but also social and language challenges of farmers in Pakistan.

heading: Requirement Elicitation & Analysis:
content: This step involves gathering both functional and non-functional requirements while focusing on farmers’ needs such as regional language support, offline usage, voice features, weather updates, and sensor data. User and business requirements are documented to guide development.

heading: System Design:
content: UI/UX mock-ups for the mobile app are created, the backend architecture and database schema are defined, and the data flow from IoT sensors to Firebase and the app is planned.

heading: Mobile App Development (Flutter):
content: The mobile application is built using Flutter with content in local languages. Voice-to-text and text-to-speech features are added for farmers with low literacy, and offline coaching using Hive or SQLite ensures the app works without an internet connection.

heading: Backend, Clouds & ML Integration:
content: Firebase Firestore is used for real-time data, Firebase authentication handles secure logins through phone or email, and Firebase Storage stores farming-related images and videos.  Historical and streaming data is processed by a cloud-based Machine Learning module that creates insights such as recommendations for crops, irrigation time, and pests and disease detection. The insights are then provided as input to the Decision Support System that involves decision rules and models for customized recommendations through the app to the farmer.

heading: IoT Sensor Integration:
content: pH and moisture sensors are connected using Arduino or ESP32. Data is transferred to Firebase using MQTT or HTTP protocols and displayed in real time on the app for farmers to monitor field conditions.

heading: DSS & Weather API Integration:
content: We use trusted weather APIs for giving local current weather, early warnings, and environmental information. The DSS is valuable where water use decisions need to be taken on the spot, decisions on planting, and avoiding extreme weather conditions such as heat waves, frost, or heavy rainfall etc.

heading: Farmer–Company Marketplace:
content: Farmers can browse, and purchase verified products like seeds, fertilizers, and pesticides, and communicate directly with vendors through a chat feature.

heading: Query Portal:
content: Farmers can send questions using text, voice, or plant images. Experts or AI provide answers, which are stored to build a useful FAQ section for future reference.

heading: Validation and Testing:
content: Android automated testing is performed along with integration testing for IoT devices, APIs, and backend systems. Pilot testing with a group of rural farmers ensures the system works effectively in real conditions.

heading: Deployment and Maintenance:
content: The application is deployed by releasing APKs for Android. NGO workers and extension officers are trained for distribution in rural areas, and Firebase Admin is used to manage regular updates and improvements. Figure 2: A roadmap of completing the PAKFASAL application

heading: Abstract
content: With the rapid advancement of Internet of Things (IoT) technology, energy monitoring systems have evolved to offer more efficient, accurate, and accessible solutions. This project presents the design and implementation of an IoT-based intelligent three-phase energy analyzer capable of measuring and analyzing key electrical parameters in real time. The system utilizes the ESP32 microcontroller along with ZMPT101B voltage sensors and SCT100A current sensors to monitor phase-wise voltage, current, real power, reactive power, apparent power, power factor, frequency, phase angle, and cumulative energy consumption (kWh). The collected data is transmitted to the ThingSpeak cloud platform for real-time visualization and remote access. A user-friendly web dashboard has been developed to display the data graphically and numerically, allowing users to track energy usage trends, view reports, and download consumption history. Firebase Authentication is integrated to enable secure login and personalized access for each user. The system eliminates the limitations of conventional energy meters by offering enhanced analytical capabilities, remote accessibility, and phase-wise monitoring, making it suitable for both residential and industrial applications. The proposed solution contributes to energy awareness and efficiency by empowering users with detailed, actionable insights into their electricity consumption. heading: Overview
content: Given that global energy demand is increasing, being smart about energy today is more valuable than ever. A lack of real-time tracking of both power generation and use has caused an energy crisis in Pakistan as well. One of the biggest challenges in Pakistan comes from energy crises which exist largely because energy use is not regularly tracked. That is even truer in industrial and commercial zones, as three-phase supply systems give more stability and efficiency. However, conventional meters are unable to provide us with the necessary information to look after and control the systems properly. Traditional energy meters only track total energy used and leave users unsure about how and why they use electricity. As technology keeps improving, energy management is now important for saving money, saving resources and supporting sustainability. One purpose of the IOT enabled smart energy analyzer is to help create lasting and effective energy solutions. Thanks to IoT, energy management will improve as you can access and analyze data from anywhere and see the results in real time. This project will develop a smart energy analyzer powered by IoT that measures usage and sends back additional information to the person using it. Because of this analyzer, consumers can check how much energy they use and how they can reduce it and their electric bill. Users can also see real-time data for every phase and review past data to lower their energy usage by knowing when to reduce energy.

heading: Problem Statement
content: In industrial and commercial settings, three-phase power networks are widely used, yet traditional energy meters offer only basic monitoring capabilities and lack real-time insights into critical parameters such as voltage, current, power factor, and various types of power (real, reactive, and apparent). This results in several challenges, including inefficient monitoring where anomalies like voltage imbalances and overloads go undetected, limited data accessibility due to the absence of remote access, poor energy optimization stemming from inadequate data, and the inability to integrate with modern smart energy management technologies. Therefore, there is a pressing need for an innovative, IoT-based system that bridges the gap between conventional energy monitoring and intelligent energy control by providing real-time data visualization, remote accessibility, and comprehensive analysis to enhance the performance and efficiency of three-phase systems. Such a system can empower users to make informed decisions, reduce energy waste, and improve operational reliability. By leveraging sensor integration and cloud-based dashboards, it enables proactive energy management from any location. Ultimately, this approach supports sustainability goals and aligns with the growing demand for smarter, more efficient energy solutions.

heading: Motivation
content: Because more energy is being used around the world and because we must be smarter about using energy, better energy management is essential. Because they are standard in industry and business, three-phase power systems depend on advanced tools to keep track of and analyze electrical data properly. Yet, classic energy meters do not give the detailed and real-time data needed to use energy most efficiently. This project is motivated by several important factors: Energy Efficiency: As costs for energy rise and we become more aware of the environment, optimizing how we use energy has become very important. A system with instant information and easy-to-use advice lets users locate energy-saving opportunities. Technological Advancements: Remote monitoring, data analysis and automation have all become possible because of IoT technology. IoT combined with energy analysis can turn traditional power management into an intelligent and flexible process. System Reliability: Damage and loss can occur in an industry when anomalies such as overloaded systems or a difference in voltages cause equipment to fail. Being able to monitor your systems in real time helps you find concerns early and make maintenance cheaper. Sustainability Goals: As we focus on sustainability, there is greater stress on using technologies that help save energy and protect the environment. An IoT-based energy analyzer helps meet these goals by promoting better energy use. Empowering Users: Helping users grasp how their energy consent is used helps them choose what actions to take, including reducing expenses, raising system performance or switching to renewable energy. To tackle these motivating factors, we are developing a strong, IoT-connected energy analyzer for three-phase systems that can help address modern issues in energy management.

heading: Objectives
content: The goal is to design and build an IoT smart energy analyzer for three-phase electrical systems. Our main objectives are: Real Time Monitoring: Users can view different electrical parameters including voltage and current of the different phases, real power, apparent power, reactive power, frequency, power factor, and energy. IoT Integration: Having an IoT system, users can look over and manage the energy analyzer from any place with a cloud portal. User-Friendly Web Interface: Allow them to use a web platform to check how much energy is being consumed in each of the three stages, review past data, analyze their energy consumption and decide on more energy-saving strategies. Enhanced Energy Efficiency: Help users to figure out which areas they use too much or too little energy. Sustainability and Efficiency: Help people manage their energy by introducing new practices that are environmentally friendly.

heading: Literature Review
content: The need to have efficient energy management, as well as fast-growing technology, has since given rise to the development of the traditional energy meters into smart energy analyzers. The current generation of the devices performs an important task, as it allows achieving accurate billing, constant 24/7 real-time monitoring, and the ability of integration with renewable energy sources. The use of smart energy analyzers combined with modern hardware devices, the IoT online services and network communication standards allows to ease the energy consumption monitoring and controlling process. Although they provide remarkable benefits associated with automation, data ease of access, and efficient functioning, they also have some challenges that include issues of privacy, reliance on constant internet access, and exorbitant costs of installation. The new developments in this area examine the enhancement of security, accuracy, and scalability of the system besides outlining the challenges. The literature shows the potential of smart energy analyzers to change energy management towards greater sustainability and sustainable management through the movement to smarter, and data-driven power systems.

heading: Conventional Technology
content: Monitoring energy use with conventional induction and static meters has been precise so far, but they can’t handle non-linear load scenarios very well. They occur because meters cannot cover a wide range of frequencies and usually have distorted harmonics. Unlike smart meters, traditional meters are not harmed by harmonics, yet they require higher load on the circuit before they operate and are easier to meddle with. Worse yet, non-linear loads generate high-frequency harmonic currents, messing up the voltage and current signals and resulting in incorrect energy measurements. Next, it looks at measuring approaches available today such as Rogowski coils, Hall-effect sensors and CTs, because each one is different in terms of reliability and responsiveness.  During testing under distorted load, static meters were seen to differ greatly from induction meter readings[1].

heading: Electromechanical Meters
content: An electromechanical meter or an induction-type energy meter, is used to measure electrical energy due to electromagnetic induction. They include a rotating aluminum disk that is moved by eddy currents arising from the interaction of voltage and current coils. As energy is used, the disk turns, and each movement is registered by the device’s mechanical counter. They are reliable tools but are less accurate than new electronic meters and don’t have features like remote monitoring.

heading: Electronic Meter
content: Digital technology helps electronic energy meters to measure electrical energy accurately. They rely on microcontrollers and sensors to read the voltage, current, power and energy being consumed which are then presented on a display screen. These new meters are not just improved but also give better results and last longer than traditional types.

heading: Hybrid Meter
content: They use both mechanical and digital systems to deliver better performance than traditional meters. Their measuring works by first passing the device through a rotating disk and then turning it over to a digital system to get precise results. Features such as data logging and monitoring when the solar system is used become possible through electronic components. They bring together the toughness and straightforwardness of electromechanical devices, while at the same time providing the exactness and added features of electronic solutions.

heading: Smart Meters
content: Smart meters stand out by letting users monitor their energy use minute by minute and by allowing them to exchange information with the company providing energy. They lead to improved accuracy in billing, allow remote viewing of system performance and offer clear data to make managing energy more efficient. Meters can do many useful things such as record time-of-use information and sense if someone is attempting to tamper with them. Homes, businesses and factories are using energy meters because it has proven to work well. Table 2. Comparison of Meters

heading: New Technologies
content: Thanks to innovation in energy measurement, we developed systems that communicate and monitor things as they happen. Since 2013, they have offered a smart system that uses GSM and ZigBee to gather usage records and allows fast two-way exchanges between customers and utilities [5]. Though the system was meant to track consumption moment by moment, initially it did not have the ability to measure power factors and harmonics. When these features do not exist, we had the need to create a system that could measure these things. Thanks to these features, energy could be managed better, and this prepared the way for new energy analyzing instruments. To evaluate power quality in modern energy systems by checking power factors and total harmonic distortion (THD) for three-phase circuits, a simulator was written in MATLAB. Because of this tool, engineers discovered that harmonic distortions could disrupt and reduce the performance of various power systems [6]. As a result, modern smart energy analyzers now routinely keep an eye on harmonic waves to ensure both reliability and efficiency in power systems. With the help of IoT technology, energy monitoring systems now serve as sophisticated analyzers. In 2017, we proposed an improvement that measured energy consumption and additionally analyzed the information, sending notices to users when there are changes [7]. With the help of IoT, it was possible to present data online for users to see and adjust their consumption. In that year, it introduced real-time harmonic analysis to its concept of energy monitoring. Thanks to IoT, the system measured three-phase Voltages and currents, and it stored and displayed the data on a web dashboard. Our IoT system spots power usage problems and adds precision with data collection which forms the core of our smart energy analyzers. Because of these features, the system offered strong accuracy in energy analysis, helping to maintain better energy use and higher standards for energy quality [8]. The growing demand for energy efficiency and lower costs in households and companies is now met by fast innovations in the Internet of Things. In addition to sensors, both an Arduino microcontroller and an ESP8266 Wi-Fi module are linked to transmit data wirelessly as it is measured. Records of historical data are stored for trend analysis and at the same time, the data is shared on the ThingSpeak platform so users can view voltage, current, power and energy in real time [9]. Its main purpose is to handle the disadvantages of classic energy monitoring which involve metering by staff, a big staff group and errors. Thanks to IoT, this method cuts both infrastructure costs and running costs while boosting accessibility and accuracy. A thorough evaluation of AMR systems has shown they depend on transmission channels such as Wi-Fi and GPRS. Even better, the suggested approach using IoT centers on Wi-Fi because it is both cheap and available everywhere. The study underlines how including solar energy and different renewable energy sources in monitoring helps improve it. For best results, you should constantly check the voltages between the solar panels and batteries. They help guide consumption and save energy by tracking and reporting on people’s behavior. Experimental tests of the suggested model confirm that energy parameters are tracked accurately and can be graphically demonstrated over time. Through real-time monitoring, examination of history and compatibility with open platforms for extra features, the system reveals how the Internet of Things can bring major improvements to energy management. The goal is also part of a greater effort to blend technology into regular life and make energy use more sustainable. IoT technology in smart meters now let’s utilities use real-time data, detect theft, control energy use and keep watch remotely, making these systems vital for managing energy. Thanks to these meters, problems seen with regular meters such as inefficiency in gathering data and vulnerability to being influenced, are eliminated. Both electricity-generating companies and their customers can now communicate as IoT allows them to monitor and control energy use precisely. By allowing data and energy to move off and on the grid, we change traditional unidirectional grids into flexible and stable smart grids [10]. Net metering and voltage protection are two features added to smart meters that increase how they function. Voltage fluctuation protection does so by cutting off power when voltage gets dangerous and turning it back on when everything is stable. Residents with solar panels can use net metering to take charge of their energy usage and offer extra energy from their system back to the grid. With these innovations, fewer gaps are seen between supply and demand on electrical networks, and more energy comes from sustainable sources. Even with progress, the industry needs to improve how IoT-based meters can connect with other devices, reduce initial prices and deal with security problems. Seeing that IoT devices may be hacked, holding secure data storage and communication is very important. It is important that all devices are standardized so they work together for more universal acceptance. Even so, modern energy management relies heavily on IoT-connected smart meters because they help save energy, cut costs and protect the environment. Things like load control, constant monitoring and two-way messages have completely transformed energy management thanks to smart energy meters (SEMs). Unlike traditional meters and AMR devices, SEMs can exchange data back and forth. Because of this, operating systems are more effective, prices can change easily, and customers have better control over energy usage. At the same time, bringing these features to devices has led to various cybersecurity risks [11]. Such SEMs are vulnerable to cyber threats such as data leaks, DDoS attacks and alterations of their devices’ firmware. Multiple security measures are used in the proposed SEM design to prevent these risks. The solution uses data encryption and a single data flow to prevent anyone from accessing vital parts of the system with technologies including LoRa WAN for long-range, secure data transfer. By using GPS modules and detectors for unauthorized access, the system becomes secure in both its data and equipment.

heading: Proposed System
content: The monitoring system we have proposed for three-phase power works more effectively and in real time than traditional energy monitoring systems. This equipment makes it possible to understand essential electrical aspects which typical meters rarely do. A strong understanding of voltage, current, power (all types) and frequency is needed for three-phase systems in both commercial and industrial areas. The sensors and microcontrollers used now ensure the system is both accurate and reliable in collecting and managing data. The key performance indicators are computed by examining actual electrical data from voltage and current sensors. Sophisticated microcontrollers such as ESP32 help make processing data fast and let devices connect easily with cloud services. As a result, users can access current information remotely whenever they need it, thanks to the updates sent automatically. The integration of these features in the suggested system helps with energy monitoring and lets users benefit from improved ways to manage energy, lower costs and optimize the system. In monitoring and controlling energy in three-phase systems today, this is a necessary tool.

heading: Overall Approach
content: The general strategy to create the IoT-based smart energy analyzer aimed at working with a three-phase system is to create an efficient and expandable solution with a user-friendly interface, allowing real-time energy monitoring and assessment. The hardware and software components in the system architecture work together to attain an accurate data capture, processing, cloud storage, and user-friendly display. To measure the important electrical parameters, initially, the system uses precise voltage and current sensors of each of the three phases. Those sensors give out analog signals that represent phase-wise voltages and current, which are input into a microcontroller (ESP32). The microcontroller is the brain, and all the real-time calculations are done on this to get information on voltages, currents, frequencies, real power (active power), apparent power, reactive power, power factor and total energy (kWh). These calculations will enable the close view of the load and energy behavior within the system. After the data is calculated, it is transmitted to the IoT ThingSpeak platform by a built-in Wi-Fi module of the ESP32. ThingSpeak is a cloud-based application which captures and keeps data of all phases in real time. It also allows graphical representation of the energy data in the form of interactive charts and plots. The dashboard is very convenient since the user can monitor it remotely using any device with an online connection, including smartphones, tablets, and PCs. To further support accessibility and usability, a purpose-built web-based dashboard was created. This site retrieves live data directly from the ThingSpeak API and displays it in a clean, responsive layout with the aid of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Energy statistics, graphical trends, and phase-wise data are individually accessible upon secure login via Firebase Authentication. Other features like dark mode, export monthly energy reports, and a "Set Point" system enable users to track, monitor, and control energy use more efficiently. This web interface provides smooth user interaction and is supplemented by IoT-based hardware installation for an end-to-end intelligent energy analysis solution.

heading: Hardware Components
content: The success of implementing the system depends greatly on having the right hardware, particularly because it needs to work in real-time. The hardware part of the project consists of the following components: Microcontroller ESP32 Voltage Sensor ZMPT101B Current Sensor SCT100A LCD Display (20x4)

heading: Microcontroller ESP32
content: The ESP32 comes with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth-based connectivity which makes it a powerful microcontroller. The system depends on it to collect information from devices, manage the data and send it to the cloud immediately to be watched. Figure . ESP32 [12]

heading: Specifications
content: Processor: Dual-core Xtensa LX6. Communication Protocols: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, UART, SPI, I2C. GPIO Pins: Supports multiple peripherals. Voltage Supply: 3.3V. Usage: Real-time data processing, IoT connectivity, and decision-making.

heading: Voltage Sensor ZMPT101B
content: The ZMPT101B is designed to measure the voltage of each phase of the generator with exactness. It is short, requires little power and gives accurate measurements the microcontroller uses.

heading: Specifications
content: Input Voltage: 250V AC Maximum Output Voltage: Analog signal proportional to the input Accuracy: Sensitive and precise data Applications: Ideal for live monitoring of voltage in power systems.

heading: Current Sensor SCT100A
content: The sensor uses the principle of a current transformer (CT) for its non-invasive operation. AC current can be measured safely and without making direct contact with electricity. Residential, commercial and industrial energy monitoring systems often use current sensors.

heading: Specifications
content: The current range is 0 to 100A for AC. The sensitivity is determined by how much you use your burden resistor (e.g., an output of 1V for 100A). The output signal at the end is analog voltage (after the burden resistor). The sensor relies on the voltage from its surroundings. Purpose: It can measure AC current without contact to be used for energy management and load investigation

heading: Implementation
content: This chapter discusses the practical deployment of the IoT Enabled Smart Energy Analyzer for Three Phase Systems. This consisted of connecting sensors, preparing the firmware, live processing data and displaying it on ThingSpeak. The purpose was to use modern instrumentation for accurate, remote observation of important electrical signals during each phase of a power system.

heading: System Architecture Overview
content: The system was designed using the following core components: ESP32 Microcontroller Voltage Sensors (3× ZMPT101B) Current Sensors (3× SCT100A) 20x4 LCD Display 5V DC Power Supply Wi-Fi for Cloud Communication EmonLib Library for Calculations ThingSpeak Platform for Data Visualization

heading: Voltage Sensing
content: Three-phase voltages are monitored using the ZMPT101B modules. These modules change the high-level AC signals into small and safe analog levels, reading which the ESP32 does with its ADC channels.

heading: Working Principle
content: The voltage sensors (ZMPT101B) are employed to read the voltage of all three phases. The ZMPT101B sensors are wired to the GPIO36, GPIO34, and GPIO32 respectively. Each of the ZMPT101B modules accepts high-voltage AC and provides a scaled-down analog output which is safe to read by the ESP32. The analog outputs permit the ESP32 to always read the voltage of each phase. Figure . Breadboard View of PTs

heading: Current Sensing
content: The SCT-100A is designed to measure current without using an invasive approach which it achieves using the CT principle. It can measure AC current remotely which safely keeps electrical contact from occurring. You will find it commonly in energy monitoring systems for both home, business and manufacturing operations. Figure . Breadboard view of CTs

heading: Working Principle
content: CT sensors or SCT100A are the current sensors used to detect the current in every phase. These outputs are linked to GPIO39, GPIO35 and GPIO33 for phases 1, 2 and 3 on the ESP32. A sensor converts the current going through it into a small analog signal of voltage. The ESP32, supported by EmonLib, uses signals to determine current, power and energy readings.

heading: ESP32 Microcontroller
content: ESP32 serves as the central unit, responsible for: Reading analog sensor data Performing calculations using the EmonLib library Displaying results on the LCD Sending processed data to ThingSpeak via Wi-Fi

heading: Working Principle
content: The ESP32 microcontroller is the central part of this development board. It takes in analog voltage and current from sensors plugged into its pins. The ESP32 operates with 5V that is regulated by a regulated power circuit containing a bridge rectifier, filtering capacitors and a 7805 IC. All the sensors and LCD display use regulated 5V power.

heading: LCD Display
content: A 20x4 LCD is included to show live data such as: Voltage and current for each phase

heading: Power Factor
content: Energy Consumption (kWh) Values are refreshed in cycles to display data from all three phases.

heading: Working Principle
content: A 20x4 LCD display is a normal alphanumeric screen that can show a maximum of 80 characters all at once (20 characters on each of 4 lines). It uses a parallel communication interface and is widely employed in embedded systems for displaying ongoing data such as voltage, current and the whole system’s status. Raster graphics are dependable and work well when you want to display more information.

heading: Power Supply
content: A 5V regulated power supply (based on an AC-DC adapter and AMS1117/LM7805 regulator) is used to power the ESP32 and sensors. Adequate filtering capacitors and safety features (diodes) are included. Figure . Breadboard view of LCD display

heading: Implementation of the Website
content: The Smart Energy Analyzer website was created to monitor and show real time energy data of three phases. It was developed by using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript on the frontend and Firebase as authentication. Sensors measured the data and transmitted it to ThingSpeak cloud channels with the help of an ESP32 microcontroller. This data is subsequently fetched and displayed on the website.

heading: Frontend Development
content: The interface of the websites has been made simple, clean and mobile-friendly. We used: HTML to organize the content. CSS to design the pages, capable of dark mode. JavaScript to handle user interactions and data fetching from the cloud. The main pages include: 1. Login and Signup Page: The user will have to create an account or log in via Firebase Authentication. The dashboard is available to authorized users only. Figure . Sign up and login page Dashboard Page: The home page on which cards and charts are used to represent energy information. It contains: Voltage, Current and Power real-time graphs. Selective buttons to view Phase 1, Phase 2 or Phase 3 data. Dark mode switches to improve the view. Sidebar for navigation (e.g., Set Point, KWh History, Change Password, Logout).

heading: Backend Integration
content: We implemented Firebase Authentication to address user login/signup, we store session data, and in the process allows users to remain logged in on different devices. Firebase deals with secure user sign-in, and log-out. We started with local storage of user sessions but later, we moved to Firebase to ensure a more secure connection and cross-device login.

heading: Data Handling
content: ESP32 reads voltage and current from sensors and computes power and energy. It transfers this data to ThingSpeak, which saves it into three different channels based on phases. The site retrieves this information from ThingSpeak via ThingSpeak API. Charts for presenting energy parameters over time are created with Chart.js. We find energy consumption history by determining the variation of total energy values at two points of time.

heading: Additional Features
content: KWh History Modal: Displays past energy consumption data in a popup style. Data Export: Users can download energy data as a Pdf file for reports. Responsive Design: The website adjusts to different screen sizes including mobiles and tablets. This website represents a full front-end and back-end facility to enable monitoring of three-phase energy usage in a remote location. It has got an easy operation, is safe with Firebase authentication, and it graphically displays real-time data of the IoT energy analyzer system.

heading: Calibration and Testing
content: Sensors were calibrated using: Things like bulbs and heaters are known as resistive loads. A range of load situations was used to test the system’s accuracy and stability.

content: The entire system was installed in an enclosure designed to be efficient and compact. The enclosure included connectors for the three-phase power and load. This facilitates remote monitoring of the three-phase electrical consumption, rendering the system appropriate for smart grid and industrial energy analysis. heading: Conclusion
content: In our project, we developed and implemented a smart energy analyzer for a three-phase system using low-cost equipment and the Internet, making it possible for real-time monitoring. Combining the Wi-Fi features of ESP32 DevKit V1 with the ZMPT101B voltage sensor and the SCT100A current sensor allowed us to get and show data on power consumption on both a display and on ThingSpeak. The prototype for a single-phase circuit proved the approach and its transfer to a three-phase system verified our belief in the system’s flexibility and dependability. During development, making sure the sensors were correctly adjusted guaranteed they remained accurate, while using the open-source dashboard allowed users to see how much energy they used over time. The use of readily available tools makes it possible for the solution to be used broadly and affordably in residential, business and small-scale industrial environments.

heading: Future work
content: As a result, this system forms a strong base for upcoming features such as auto fault detection, detailed analysis of energy use and predictive warnings for maintenance. It would be possible to enhance the system by detecting anomalies with machine learning, including support for solar panels and allowing the client to monitor from mobile apps. As a result, this project meets its target of helping users save energy and money, while also suggesting ways to make the grid more intelligent and connected so all stakeholders can base their decisions on helpful data.

heading: Skills Learned
content: This Project entitled "IoT-Enabled Smart Energy Analyzer for Three-Phase Systems" helped us learn about embedded systems, how to integrate IoT and ways to analyze power in three-phase systems. We worked with the ESP32, ZMPT101B voltage sensor and SCT100A current sensor, discovering how to calibrate sensors, collect correct data and transmit the data online to ThingSpeak. I learned to design circuits, use sensors and handle display screens, also coding in the C/C++ languages. Developing the project gave me a clearer picture of both three-phase systems and real-time energy monitoring. My skills in dealing with problems, handling projects, working with others and making technical documentation all improved as we completed our project in 10 months.

heading: Project Abstract
content: Increasing digitalization in Pakistan's treasury or real-estate markets has created a need for an efficient management system. However, many developers still rely on outdated spreadsheets and gross accounting software, which, while expensive, are not the focus of the work files of the prime ministers and real-state leaders. In response to these failures, the project has promoted the development of web-based Accounting or Property management system specifically designed for local real-state companies. This system combines rental interest management, self-analysis of leases, tracking of transactions, or financial reporting into a single interface, thus allowing for a smooth transition between financial and property operations. It also includes a public portal that displays offered residential and commercial units, grouped by city and location, with real-time backend database synchronization. Compared with commercial products like QuickBooks, which require paid subscriptions and don't offer customization toward local requirements, our system is affordable and local-tailorable, with capacity for any number of users. The final product's ultimate goal is the achievement of better operational efficiency, reduction in manual workloads, and increment in transparency in property and financial management among real estate businesses.

heading: Introduction
content: Digital change of sustainable business growth is essential. Despite this change, a large portion of small and medium developers still depends on manual book keeping and basic accounting tools, which limit their ability to effectively manage financial and operational data [1]. This dependence often causes errors, copy of data, and delays in financial reporting, which causes difficulty monitoring rental income, tenants' liabilities, and salary activities.

heading: Problem Statement
content: Current trade accounting systems such as QuickBooks provide strong financial features but are not specifically designed for the property sector. They lack module for lease management, tenant billing, and rent contract automation, which forcing businesses to use multiple disconnected tools to complete the basic workflow. In addition, these commercial platforms are expensive, requires subscription licensing, and limit the number of consumers, which makes them unacceptable to local property developers.

heading: Project Objectives
content: To develop a customized web-based platform integrating accounting and property management in a single environment. To automate key business operations such as rental registration, lease tracking, rent invoicing, payroll management, and financial reporting. To build a public property listing portal that dynamically updates available commercial and residential units in real time. To ensure transparency and eliminate data inconsistencies between internal accounting records and public property information. To implement the system using Laravel (PHP framework) and MySQL for scalability, security, and modular design. To design a user-friendly and responsive web interface accessible across multiple devices. To provide a cost-effective and locally manageable alternative to commercial accounting platforms. To enhance data accuracy, reduce manual workload, and support the digital transformation of Pakistan’s real estate businesses.

heading: Open and Customizable Business Management Systems
content: Recent research on small business management systems indicates a growing shift toward open and configurable software architectures that compete with proprietary tools in both performance and flexibility.[2] These systems offer essential accounting features such as double-entry bookkeeping, financial reporting, and automated ledger management while eliminating the licensing restrictions imposed by commercial software. This trend reflects a broader trend toward flexible and cost-effective platforms that enable organizations to control financial processes without external constraints.

heading: ERP Solutions in the Real Estate Sector
content: Within the real estate sector, advanced Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) solutions have sought to strengthen the real estate data with project and logistics modules [3]. It is understood that the application of ERP to the main domain improves the intermediation of workflows, facilitates automatic rent receipts, and facilitates payroll tracking across the real estate sector [4]. However, most ERP systems are built for large-scale corporations and require significant technical expertise and financial resources to deploy, making them unsuitable for small or medium-sized developers working in tight time slots.

heading: Digital Property Portals and User Experience
content: In contrast to other platforms, digital property portals have reinvented the way to access and manage real estate. Platforms like Zameen.com have developed and enhanced user interfaces, detailed property filters, or real-time tracking apps, enabling surfers to search for property based on location, type or price.[5] Other platforms have established a standard for the proper use or design of property management systems. The interactive features of such portals, including responsive layouts and location-based search tools, serve as inspiration for the user interface of our system’s property listing module.

heading: Research Gap and System Justification
content: Despite these innovations, there is a difference in these solutions that connect the financial accounting automation with property management and public listings in the same integrated platform. Current tools are either focused on financial works or property incomplete listings, but not both. The purpose of our system is to eliminate the gap by providing a united, web-based solution that automatically, manages payroll, and harmonizes property data in real time. This approach is in line with the current direction of research and industrial exercise, while Pakistani real estate firms solve the specific operational needs.

heading: Architecture
content: The proposed system will follow the client server architecture [6], which will ensure central data management, security and scalability. A dedicated server running Laravel and SQL will handle data processing, verification, and business logic, while client web browsers will securely access the application. Both management users and public visitors will discuss with their respective modules through a separate verification control interface. This structure allows many users to work simultaneously without compromising the integrity of the data.

heading: Backend Development
content: We will implement Laravel modules for payroll computation, recurring rent invoicing, lease contract creation and financial reporting. Apply double entry accounting principles to ensure accurate Balance Sheets and Ledger Management. Develop an automatic Monthly Invoice generation and schedule mechanism for reminder.

heading: Frontend Development
content: Design a responsive dashboard that facilitates navigation for non -technical users and provides immediate access to key modules. Ensure compatibility in multiple devices and browsers using modern frontend framework. heading: ABSTRACT
content: Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) is a popular software engineering practice that specifies system behavior in natural language, fostering collaboration between developers, testers, and business stakeholders. By separating specifications from implementations, BDD enables clearer communication, better requirement validation, and improved test-driven workflows, making it a widely adopted approach in modern quality assurance. However, BDD test suites are not free from challenges, as poorly designed scenarios often lead to “test smells,” which undermine readability, increase brittleness, and reduce long-term maintainability. Existing research primarily addresses test smells at the implementation level, leaving the specification level underexplored due to the complexity of analyzing natural language. To address this gap, this project proposes an NLP-based approach that preprocesses BDD specifications through tokenization, stopword removal, and lemmatization, and extracts linguistic, contextual, and domain-specific features such as part-of-speech tags, named entities, BDD keywords, action words, and parameters. These features are then mapped to corresponding test code elements using an NLP-driven algorithm, which simultaneously enables systematic detection of test smells like duplication, ambiguity, and overly complex steps. Empirical case studies are employed to validate the model, demonstrating improved accuracy in mapping specifications to implementations and enhanced smell detection capabilities. The expected outcomes include better traceability between specifications and tests, improved test maintainability, and higher overall quality assurance in BDD environments, contributing a novel methodology that integrates NLP into automated software testing practices.

heading: Introduction
content: Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) is a software development methodology. It was first presented by Daniel et al., on the idea to clearly define what the software should do before creating it. This method avoids confusion by clearly stating what the software should do, helping it meet business requirements and keeping everyone on the same page. The two levels of tests  are the implementation level and the specification level as shown in Figure 1. A Domain-Specific Language (DSL) like Gherkin is used to write natural language-based scenarios at the specification level. This allows requirement engineers, developers, and testers to all have an understanding of the system. Developers write test code to make sure the system does what the written requirements say. BDD is used a lot in research and business because it helps everyone on the team stay connected and understand each other . Among the most widely used tools that support creating, organizing, and running BDD tests are frameworks like Robot , SpecFlow, Cucumber, and Gauge. These frameworks preserve a direct link to executable test code while enabling the specification of system behavior in natural language. Although BDD enhances system validation and communication, its two-level architecture creates new difficulties for test design and upkeep. In particular, it becomes more difficult to guarantee uniformity and quality at both levels when specifications and implementations are kept apart. One of the major challenges in BDD is the emergence of test smells, which are symptoms of poor test design that reduce readability, increase brittleness, and complicate maintenance . Test smells have been studied extensively in unit testing and code-level implementations , where automated detection tools exist to identify common smells like Assertion Roulette or Eager Test. However, most of these studies are limited to the implementation level and do not address the unique challenges of natural language specifications. For example, a specification scenario may include duplicated steps, vague action descriptions, or ambiguous requirements that introduce specification-level smells. Detecting such smells is difficult due to the flexible and natural language-based nature of BDD specifications . Although previous research has explored requirement smells using Although NLP-based methods  exist, we have seen limited application of similar methods in the analysis of BDD scenarios. This ultimately results in test suites that gradually lose their quality, reducing their ability to ensure correctness of software behavior, and increasing long-term maintenance costs. All of the test smell definitions used in this proposal, are taken from a systematic mapping study of test smell detection tools . By introducing an NLP-based method to map BDD specifications to their corresponding implementation tests and automatically identify test smells at the specification level, this project seeks to address these issues. Tokenisation, stopword removal, and lemmatisation are used to preprocess BDD specifications at the start of the methodology. While domain-specific features like BDD keywords ("Given," "When," "Then"), action words, and parameters are found to improve the mapping process, linguistic features like dependency parses, named entities, and part-of-speech tags are extracted to capture the grammatical structure of scenarios. An NLP-driven mapping algorithm that uses similarity metrics like cosine similarity on vectorised features is then used to align these extracted features with test code elements. This alignment creates traceability from natural language scenarios to implementation tests, as well as helps identify smells, such as duplication of steps, overly complicated scenarios. The project aims to deliver a proven approach to improve the quality of BDD tests, focusing on traceability and identifying test smells. This approach will be evaluated through real-world BDD projects using empirical methods. Anticipated results include higher maintainability of test suites, reduced brittleness in test cases, and improved readability of specifications. Furthermore, this research contributes to advancing automated quality assurance by integrating NLP with BDD testing practices. The success criteria will be based on measurable improvements in smell detection accuracy, successful mapping of specifications to implementations, and evidence of improved maintainability through refactoring efforts. Ultimately, this project provides a practical solution that not only identifies quality issues early at the specification level but also strengthens the overall reliability of BDD test frameworks.

heading: Problem Statement
content: Many test smells have been introduced in the literature but with a limited scope, i.e., their definitions are limited to Unit-testing. Multi-level test cases in BDD have not been considered during defining test smells. Up to our knowledge, we have not found any study that discuss the scope of test smells in BDD domain. There might be a reason that this direction has been less focused by the researchers, maybe the way we write specifications in BDD. For example, the specification writer has freehand to write test specifications in natural language by not even following any syntax writing standards. As specification syntax varies from person to person, which also made it difficult to define test smell definitions at this level. That’s why, its hard to define test smell definitions at this level. Similarly, another very famous BDD based testing framework Cucumber use Gherkin language to write specifications. Although, there are some standard rules of Given, When, Then, And are supposed to be followed. For further analysis of test smells in this project, we will consider Gauge framework as a case study, which is quite famous and young testing framework. All of the test smell definitions used in this article, are taken from a systematic mapping study of test smell detection tools .

content: The main focus area of the project deals with the NLP based mapping of BDD specification for detection of test smells in test cases. To this end, we shall: To collect a curated dataset of BDD specifications for empirical analysis. To develop an NLP-based system for mapping BDD specifications to test code. To introduce an approach for detecting test smells at the specification level. To introduce the mechanism that detect the mapping smells from specifications to implementation. To analyze the result and compare with the state-of-the-art tools that detect smells.

heading: Related work
content: The related work is mainly focused on the systematic literature reviews over the past few years, and it has shown that TDD and BDD has been widely used and researched. Many researcher promote the adoption of BDD based testing because of its effectiveness and support for business modeling people involved in the system testing. It is widely known that test smells negatively affect the program code quality , and therefore many studies have been proposed to automatically identify and remove test smells from the test cases especially at source code level . But there are very less studies found that draw an attention towards test smells considerations at BDD specification level. Islam et al.  claims that the BDD is lacking of standard methods and techniques for identifying and Refactoring the test smells. Binamungu et al.  wrote a thesis on detecting the duplication’s of specification from the BDD frameworks. In his thesis he proposed a framework that detects duplicate scenarios from the specification based on the comparison of its characteristics, that were extracted from the scenario executions. His main focus was on production patterns used by each scenario, and consider the other (duplicate) scenario as a smell if it has the same execution functionality. The author Causevic et al.  highlighted that several experienced developers took comparatively very less time to finish test driven task than the in comparison with a new user. However, for an inexperienced person it would be fast to write BDD based testing specifications. The benefit of using BDD based testing lies when the team collaborate, allowing everyone in the team representing to write test cases for system under test. Abushama et al.  have examined several important aspects of BDD vs TDD regrading their success rate by considering different factors, i.e., cost, time, and quality, which shows the customer satisfaction.
