heading: 2.1.1 Topology
content: Neural networks are designed in an input -output manner. there are diverse hidden layers in - between input neuron layer and output neuron layer. The input layer picks up the input signals in form of weights and passes them on to ‘hidden’ layers, these hidden layers will then do their thing to converge or connect the input to the required output (Figure 4).  There are many ways to link neurons(nodes) with each other in the neural networks, it is observed that applying different node linking strategies show different behaviour in results. The most promising and simple neural network topology is the feed-forward network. The neurons (nodes) send  signals in only one direction as illustrated in the figure there are no loops or cycles in feed-forward network. Figure 4: A simple  Neural Network

heading: 2.1.2 Mechanism
content: Like humans, the first thing that a NN has to do is learn. The learning process require huge amount of training data which is used in any of three ways described below to train a network Supervised learning: One of the easiest and most used way of learning is supervised learning, which requires a large set of data with known results. Then the learning goes like this: Process one dataset. Compare the output against the known result. Adjust the network -as in weights- and repeat. Unsupervised learning: This involves data that may not have known results. It is possible to derive some kind  of cost function from the behaviour observed with random initial results. The cost function tells the neural network how much it is off the target. The network then can adjust its parameters on the fly while working on the real data. Reinforced learning: Unlike in supervised learning where training data comes with an answer key, which is manually created by humans, in reinforcement learning, there is no answer key. Network has to decide how to act to perform its task. In the absence of existing training data, the network learns from experience. It collects the training examples and classify the data, for example [this action was good, that action was bad] through hit and try with the goal of achieving the global maxima. Over time, the network learns to pre fer the right kind of action and to avoid the wrong one.

heading: 2.2 Perceptron:
content: A perceptron is basically an artificial neuron  made to apply algorithm that enables supervised learning of binary classifiers.  A binary classifier converges the inputs into exactly two outputs (true/false or yes/no etc.). It is also defined as a linear classifier, due to the fact that it makes its predictions based on linear predictor function combining a set of weights with the feature vector. Figure 5 show the basic structure of a perceptron and its role in a NN. Figure 5: Perceptron in NN

heading: 2.2.1 Perceptron Algorithm
content: Working of a perceptron is done in three basic steps, i.e. (1) Input scaling (2) Input summation and introducing bias. (3) Activation function. 1. Input scaling: We obtain input data by multiplying the weight value assigned to particular input in the form of vectors. To take an example if we have five input neurons we assign each input neuron their individuals weights which are re- adjustable in attempt to decrease the calculated error in preceding iteration. 2. Input summation and introducing bias: After the modification of inputs by scaling the input signals are added up to obtain a single value and a Bias called offset value is added to total sum. In the learning phase the Bias values are readjusted at the end of each iteration. In the start of first iteration all the neurons are initialized with random weights and biases and to decrease the deviation from desired outpu t, the weights and biases are gradually changed. This way the designed neural network moves towards our desired state and learn patterns we wish.

heading: 3. Activation Function:
content: Lastly, the above described additions and calculations done with neurons is turned into the final (output) signal. the input signals from examples of training data, combines them with weights and bias into a linear equation - the activation function: activation = Σ (weights * input Data) + bias There is a lot of basal anatomy of an activation function It is a simple bifold function that has alone two accessible results. This function returns 1 if the input is absolute or zero, and 0 for any negative input (see Figure 6). The activation is again adapted into an output value or prediction application using an alteration function such as the step alteration function. The weights of the Perceptron algorithm can be calculated from training data using the gradient descent approach. Figure 6: A binary function

heading: 2.2.2 Gradient Descent
content: Gradient Descent is the action of decreasing a function by subsequently following the gradients of the cost function. This involves alive the anatomy of the cost and its derivative so that from an accustomed point you apperceive the gradient can move in that direction, e.g. decline appears in the minimum value. The way this enhancement algorithm works is that every training instance is apparent to the model one at a time. The model makes an anticipation for a training instance, the absurdity is calculated, and the archetypal is adapted in adjustment to abate the absurdity for the next instance (as discussed in the previous section). This action can be acclimated to find the set of weights in a model that aftereffect in the smallest error for the model on the training data.

heading: 2.2.3 Convergence
content: The perceptron is a direct (linear) classifier, so if the training dataset is not linearly separable, accordingly it will never get to the accompaniment with all its input vectors c lassified accurately adjoin their corresponding outputs, that is the absolute examples cannot be abundantly afar from the abrogating examples by a hyperplane (Figure 7). Thus, inputs cannot be absolutely mapped to audible outputs beneath standard learning algorithm, resulting in a complete abortion to learn. If the training set is linearly separable, again the perceptron is affirmed to converge. Figure 7: Linearly Separable data

content: 2.3 Backpropagation. With a single perceptron, changing the weights according to the error finding, while achieving the task and more specifically convergence is quite simple. But when there are multiple neurons having numerous connections in a different layer of the network.  Adjusting the weights,  for each perceptron or connection that contributes to the overall error of the network, is a complicated task. Therefore, backpropagation is a solution to improv e the weights of a multi -layered network. In backpropagation the network output is generated exactly the way output of perceptron is generated the network inputs are first multiplied by the weights then the inputs are added into a single value to forward through the network. The main difference that effects is that before reaching the output the network is passed through some additional layers. While training the networks weights are re-adjust according to error value, therefore the error value must be passed back through the network. Ultimately the least or the final error value is responsible to fine-tune the weights of all connection in the network.

heading: 2.4 Convolutional Neural Networks
content: Convolutional Neural Networks(CNN) is a sub-class of Neural Networks, based on a feed-forward architecture and contains one or more convolutional layers with fully connected layers. It’s not necessary to use extra layers like pooling and max pooling layers but tied weights are commonly used in CNNs. The most appropriate usage of CNNs is processing of two-dimensional data and specifically visual pro cessing applications. However, CNNs have recently generated ground-breaking results in speech and image processing. These networks can be trained using many different techniques including the baseline backpropagation technique. Compared to feed forward and deep neural networks it is easier to train CNNs by using few initial parameters. the most robust application is video recognition and real time natural language processing. compared to other image classification algorithms  specifically the image classification problem CNNs require incredibly less pre -processing. The major advantage CNNs have over other algorithms is that they are independent and does not require prior knowledge.

heading: 2.4.1 Architecture
content: A CNN architecture is formed by assemblage of distinct layers that transform the input aggregate into an output aggregate through a differentiable function. A CNN consists of an input and an output layer, and assorted hidden layers. The hidden layers of a CNN contain convolutional layers, pooling layers, affiliated (connected) layers and standardization layers.

heading: Convolutional Layer
content: Basically, convolutional layers perform an operation on input said to be convolutional operation and pass the result to the succeed ing layer. Free parameters are reduced by this operation hence allow networks to have few parameters and more depth. Unfortunately, it is not practically feasible to connect all the neurons in the previous layer to every neuron in next layer so to make it happen a local connectivity is established that maps a small portion of input volume to each neuron. the receptive field controls this neuron connection. As a result, each neuron is connected to only a small region of the input volume. This connection is controlled by the receptive field of the neuron. The connections are along x and y axis (width and height) and spread along the full depth of the input volume. Figure 8 shows  this connectivity arrangement. Figure 9: Connection of a Neuron and Receptive field

heading: 21 of 63  09 January 2018
content: There are three key parameters that control the output volume size of the convolutional layer is controlled by: the depth, stride and zero-padding. The depth of the output volume controls the number of neurons in a layer that affix to the same region of the input volume. These neurons apprentice to actuate for altered appearance in the input. The allocation of spatial dimensions (height and width) is controlled by stride. for the stride value of 1we move the filters one pixel at a time. This leads to heavily overlapping acceptant fields and, ultimately, ample achievement volumes. When the stride is 2 (or rarely 3 or more) again the filters jump 2 pixels at a time as th ey accelerate around. The acceptant fields overlap less, and the consistent output volume has decreased spatial dimensions. Sometimes it is acceptable to pad the input with zeros on the bound of the input volume. The admeasurement of this padding is a thir d hyperparameter. padding provides ascendancy of the output volume spatial size. In particular, sometimes it is adorable to absolutely bottle the spatial size of the input volume.

heading: Pooling Layer
content: The pooling layer combines the outputs of neuron clusters from one layer and transforms or ‘pools’ them into a single neuron for the next layer. It helps to gradually reduce the spatial size of the representation, to reduce the number of parameters and amount of computation in the network. There are two types of pooling techniques under discussion: Max pooling This pooling uses the maximum value from each cluster of neurons is selected at the previous layer. Average pooling Uses the mean value from each of a cluster of neurons at the previous layer. Commonly, the pooling layer is introduced between succeeding convolutional layers in a CNN architecture, even though it operates individualistically on every part of the input and resizes it.

heading: Fully Connected Layer
content: Fully connected layers affix every neuron in one layer  to every neuron in additional layer. It is in assumption the same as the traditional multi -layer perceptron neural network. Neurons in a fully connected layer accept access to all activations in the previous layer, as apparent in neural networks. Their ac tivations can appropriately be computed with a cast multiplication followed by a Bias (offset).

heading: 2.4.2 CNN in Image Captioning
content: CNNs, due to their specialised architecture and the additional layers are frequently used in image classification and recognition systems. They were first used to evaluate video quality, objectively, but were trained manually and resulted in a very low root mean square error. But when CNN was applied to tasks like video captioning and facial recognition, a large decline in error rate was observed as proven by [1]. Another paper reports a 97.6 percent recognition rate on 5,600 still images of more than 10 subjects [2].  The ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge is a benchmark in object classification and detection, with mil lions of images and hundreds of object classes. Countless models are presented, and their performance is measured against humans. CNN based model was presented and evaluated and, not surprisingly the score was the closest to humans. [3] Mostly machine gen erated captions fail to classify objects that are small and have difficulty in captioning images that are not captured properly having blurred effect. On the other hand, a human can easily give captions for these images, but will have trouble categorizing objects in specific categories (particular cat breed). CNN works to eliminate both of these problems by extracting even the tiny details from an image, and correctly classifying them into categories.

heading: 2.4.3  Fine-tuning
content: There are many diverse applications that involve CNNs but for most of them there is lack of training data. normally convolutional neural networks need huge amount of data for training to avoid the effect of overfitting. Overfitting is the phenomenon where a model makes generalised predictions due to less training data available. The most common technique is to use large data sets of similar domains for training. A fter the initial training the network the parameters have converged. Now these converged parameters are more refined with an additional training using domain related datasets to fine tune network weights for better predictions. This permits convolutional networks to be productively applied to problems with small training datasets.

heading: 2.5 Recurrent Neural Networks
content: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have gained quiet a lot of popularity recently, especially in NLP related tasks. In most cases, the inputs are independent of each other and so are the outputs. But there are scenarios, mostly language based, where you have  to know the answer from the previous step to move forward. For example, if you wish to adumbrate the next word in a sentence you better apperceive which words came afore it. RNNs are alleged recurrent because they accomplish the aforementioned assignment for every aspect of a sequence, with the achievement of getting depended on the previous computations (Figure 8). Another way to think about RNNs is that they have a “memory” which store information about what has been calculated so far. In theory RNNs can make use of information in randomly long sequences, but in practice they are limited to go back only few steps. Figure 10: RNN as language generator

heading: 2.5.1 Language Modelling and Generating Text
content: Given an arrangement of words, we wish to adumbrate the probability of each word accustomed the previous words. Language Models accept us to measure how acceptable a sentence is, which is an important ascribe for Machine Translation (since high-probability sentences are almost correct). A side-effect of getting able to predict the next word is that we get generative model, which allows us to accomplish new argument by sampling from the achievement probabilities. And depending on what our training abstract is. We can accomplish all kinds of stuff. The applications of language models are two-fold: First, it allows us to account approximate sentences based on how acceptable they are to action in the absolute world. This gives us an admeasurement of grammatical and semantic correctness. Such models are about acclimated as share of Machine Translation systems. Secondly, language model allows us to accomplish new argument Training a language model on John Gresham allows us to accomplish Gresham-like text.

heading: 2.5.2 Training
content: Training a RNN uses the backpropagation algorithm, just  like a traditional Neural Network. However, it applies minor changes on the parameters because they are shared by all the steps in the network, the slope at each output depends not only on the current step, but also the previous time steps. For example, in order to calculate the gradient at, say g=5,  the model will need to backpropagate four steps back and sum up the gradients. This phenomenon is commonly known as Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT). Sometimes, RNNs trained with BPTT will encounter difficulty going back. This happens when long -term dependencies are encountered which are simply dependencies with steps that are far apart. To avoid this problem, modified RNNs, such as the LSTMs are available

heading: 2.5.3 RNN Extensions
content: Over the years researchers have developed more sophisticated types of RNNs to deal with some of the shortcomings of the RNN model. Two such extensions are discussed below Bidirectional RNNs are based on the idea that the output at time  may not only depend on the previous elements in the sequence, but also future elements. For example, to predict a missing word in a sequence you want to look at both the  left and the right context. Bidirectional RNNs are quite simple. They are just two RNNs stacked on top of each other. The output is then computed based on the hidden state of both RNNs. LSTMs Long Short -Term Memory networks (LSTMs) differs from traditional RNNs in that they are capable of learning long -term dependencies. Their architectures are almost similar except for the ‘memory’ advantage they enjoy. The memory which enables the LSTM to achieve this are data-structures known as cells. Cells can decide what to keep in and what to discard from the memory. As inputs, two parameters are passed. One is the value of the previous state and th e second is the current input. These two states are enough to enable LSTM to learn long -term dependencies and is the closest to memorising something by heart. The decision of what to keep and what to discard is not completely the cell’s. This decision is carefully controlled and monitored by, yet another data-structures called gates. The gate consists of a sigmoid neural net layer and a multiplication operation which allows them to put a check on the information going through. Gates are a way to optionally let information through. They are composed out of a sigmoid neural net layer and a simple multiplication operation.

content: Encoder-decoder Architecture So far, with all the work done for the task of Artificial Vision, using Neural Networks for the job has proven to be the most successful. The state of the art models (most of them) that captions images employ the encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder is used to map the input image into a numerical vector representation. The decoder part generates the actual captions in natural language using the vector representations from the encoder. This architecture allows the models to be trained end to end, meanin g that the parameters of the whole network are learned together, thereby avoiding the problem of aligning several independent components.

heading: Encoder
content: In the encoding phase of the captioning task, which is where features are extracted from the image, a convolutional neural network is applied. The output is a feature map from the CNN model which is used for classification purposes.

heading: Decoder
content: The decoder is basically a RNN, or more specifically a LSTM, which is responsible for language modelling. It is trained to predict the next word conditioned on all the previously predicted words. To make the process more efficient, the words representation is distributed. This allows the clustering of similar words, which can be retrieved in less time.

heading: 3 Related work
content: Automatic Image Captioning was first tackled using classification models which only assigned a label to an image. This approach, although very efficient, is not able to label every novel image presented to it. This is because the outputs are fixed and already defined. For an image captioning model to be perfect, the number of captions that it produces need to be, basically, unlimited. In section 3.1 we discuss how the image captioning task has evolved over time and the models that have been used. In section 3.2 methods to evaluate machine generated captions are discussed. In section 3.3 types of datasets used for image captioning tasks are presented.

heading: 3.1 Image captioning models
content: Most of the image captioning tasks are based on the two categories defined below. The models, which first detects the objects and their attributes from an image and then, using a natural language model generates a caption, are classified as Generative Models We classify them as Generative Models. The second category apply retrieval techniques to come up with the most similar captions in the training set and ranks them according to their similarity. Retrieval can be done from either Visual Space, or a Multimodal Space. Figure 11: Architecture of a Generative model

heading: 3.1.1 Generative models
content: These were the earliest models for captioning images. They work on a basic principle of directly mapping images to descriptions. Their image captioning task can be divided into two phases: object classification and sentence generation. An advantage of this approach over the other models is that it can produce novel captions to describe any image. In the first phase, CV is used to classify the image into different objects and labels. The attribute s of the objects are also identified as well as the relationship among them.  Farhadi et al., 2010 [1] and Kulkarni et al., 2011 [2] deal with the image classification task similarly by capturing different aspects of an image rather than classifying the image as a whole: the different aspects can include the objects present in the image, their attributes, the relationship between them, and the overall scene. The work of Fang et al. (2015) [3] does not require predefined classes for labelling the objects and scene type. In fact, they propose a rather smart way to train image extractors to directly associate images to their respected descriptions, which are available through different datasets (discussed in Section 3.3).

heading: 29 of 63  09 January 2018
content: The second phase, called the generation phase, processes the outputs received from the first phase. These outputs are converted to phrases and then combined to produce Natural language captions, using NLP techniques which include pre -defined word templates, n -grams and language-specific grammar rules). Kulkarni et al. (2011) [3] and Li et al. (2011) [5] propose n-gram based language models. These language models generate captions that are fluent and well formed, nut may have semantics issues and fail to produce novel captions. A second approach uses sentence templates to generate descriptions Yang et al. (2011) [2].  The templates are pre-defined frames with empty slots that are filled by the outputs generated in the first phase

heading: 3.1.2 Visual Space Retrieval Models
content: These models generate captions by retrieving images similar to the image that is being captioned . The retrieved images are already captioned; thus, their captions are used to generate a novel caption. This means that a huge amount of training data is required for the model to give good captions. Figure 12: Model architecture that retrieve image from visual space The first step is to extract visual features from the image that is to be captioned (Query image). The same CV techniques of feature extractions are used which are discussed under the generative models are used that extract features. Next, a similarity measure is used to retrieve similar images from the training set. The retrieved set of images is called the Candidate set. In the final step, the descriptions in the Candidate set are re -ranked and combined according to predefined rules,  and presented as a caption. Kuznetsova et al. (2012) [1] propose a visual space retrieval model that extracts the visual and semantic information from the input image and classifies it accordingly. The retrieval is done by querying against each of the entities detected from the query image. The retrieved images against each query instance ae used to produce a caption that satisfies the maximum numbers of detected instances. For example, if a lion is detected in the input lions, then all those descriptions or phrases

heading: 30 of 63  09 January 2018
content: are returned which are annotating images containing lions and only lions, then a final caption is generated from the retrieved phrases. The method of Gupta et al. (2012) [3] is another phrase -based approach. Instead of using visual object detectors or scene classifiers, they rely only on the textual information in the descriptions of the visually similar images to extract the visual content of the input image.

heading: 3.1.3 Multimodal Space Retrieval Models
content: The models based on this technique approaches the image captioning task as a retrieving problem, rather than a generative problem. Concept of a multi -modal space is used instead of a singular visual space. During training, the system is made to learn the multimodal space. The training data consists of images, along with their captions. Since both the visual and textual data are presented in the space, as pairs, it refers to the multimodality of the space. After the system has been trained, a query is processed by the model over the learned space and retrieves those results, in the form of image-caption pairs, which best satisfy the query. Figure 13: A multimodal space model The best thing about using a multimodal space is that it makes the model bi-directional. This means that the model can be used for captioning an image as well as retrieving the appropriate image against a query sentence. Hodosh et al. (2013) [1] proposes a model based on this technique. Their model map both images and sentences into a common space. It is then used for two tasks; image annotation given a query image and image searching given a query sentence. Karpathy & Fei -Fei, (2015) [2] base their work on this architecture, and introduce an encoder - decoder framework for visual tasks. The encoding part is where the multimodal space is constructed, and the machine learns from the image-caption pairs. The processing and ranking from the whole training set is done here. The decoding phase outputs descriptions based on the rankings.

heading: 3.2 Evaluation Methodology
content: Evaluating machine -generated capti ons has been proven to be a difficult task (Section 1.2). Traditionally, it is done by human experts, which is the most common way to assess the quality of generated captions in terms of grammar and content. However human evaluations are time taking, expensive and require bilingual experts. For this reason, a number of automatic metrics have been proposed over the years, which are cheaper and much more efficient at evaluating captions. Section

heading: 3.2.1 explains the methodology behind conducting human evaluations and section 3.2.2 describes
content: the different automatic metrics available and the techniques they apply to analyse the machine - generated captions.

heading: 3.2.1 Human Evaluation
content: Using humans to evaluate sentences or machine generated texts is the most authentic as well as being the crudest of all the methods. Basically, language experts are hired to manually judge or give their opinion on the machine generated texts. The evaluators are presented with the images and their respected captions during the whole exercise and they are told to access the quality of the captions against some strict instructions. Much of the human evaluations related to machine generated sentences is done on the Amazon Mechanical Turk. [5]. Things that have to be taken care of: • The caption is accurate in its description • The caption is grammatically correct • The caption has no incorrect information. • The caption is relevant for this image • The caption is creatively constructed • The caption is human-like.

heading: 3.2.2 Automatic Metrics
content: Evaluating machine generated texts by human evaluation is an expensive and time taking task. A lot of manual work is required, calculations required, and data managed. To make the task less lengthy and more simple, different measures and techniques have be en developed. These techniques may not prove to be as accurate in their evaluations as the human evaluations, but they are easy to implement, consistent in their scoring, liable and general purpose and provides with good comparison grounds. Such automatic metrics are discussed in this section, which are specifically designed to compare the machine generated captions against one or more human - written captions known as the reference sentences, For the ease of understanding, the machine-generated captions use d in our experiments will be referred as the set of Candidate sentences. The human-written ground-truths are referred as the set of Ground-truths or GT.

heading: BLEU
content: It is one of the earliest automatic metrics that were developed for the evaluation of machine generated sentences. It is quite basic in principle, hence quiet a generally -purposed used metric. The most popular use of BLEU is for evaluating machine generated translations, but it was the first metric to be applied on image captions. B LEU actually calculates the precision of a machine - generated caption against one reference sentence. This is done through an explicit mapping of n - gram (1 to 4 -gram) between the two sentences, calculating the precision using the mapping and finally, imposing a brevity penalty so that very short sentences or phrases can be ignored. Bleu is very efficient for measuring the fluency or the precision between two captions. To measure recall and the semantic similarity, this is not the appropriate model.

heading: METEOR
content: Meteor focuses on those evaluation criteria that were overlooked by Bleu. They use the same technique of unigram mapping, but in a more sophisticated and detailed way. The n-grams among the candidate and reference sentences are first mapped word to word, then ide ntical stems are matched (known as stemmers) and lastly words which are synonyms of each other are mapped (by using WordNet synonyms tables). After the mapping has been done, F -mean score is calculated which is computed using precisio n and recall formula. This way, they claim that they evaluate both the precision as well as recall. As recall is, by formula, improved when there is a larger number of reference sentences to  compare against, it is not wise to use METEOR in cases where there is one reference sen tence against one candidate sentence

heading: ROUGE
content: It is preferred in evaluations of textual summaries. But many variants have been developed for different tasks. Such is the variant ROUGE_L which is suitable for the purpose of image captioning. The mapping is done based on the LCS of the candidate and reference sentences. LCS or the Longest Common Subsequence is the set of the words which is present in both the sentences in the same sequence. This is almost the same as matching n -grams, but eliminates the need to specify the number of grams that are to be compared. This means that there is no limit to the number of n-grams that have to be found. After the mapping, F -measure score is calculated, which is, naturally based on the LCS. Similar to METEOR, this metric also focuses more on recall, and works well when there are large number of reference sentences. Similar strengths and weaknesses as BLEU.

heading: Cider
content: Cider is specially designed for the task of evaluating machine generated captions.  This metric is growing very popular because it gives the highest correlation with humans. It measures the amount of similarity between a candidate caption and a set of human generated captions.

heading: 3.3 Datasets
content: There is a wide range of datasets available for au tomatic image description research. The images in these datasets are associated with textual descriptions and differ from each other in certain aspects such as in size, the format of the descriptions and in how the descriptions were collected. These datase ts contain human written annotations against each image. Anyhow involves post - processing to remove spelling mistakes, and sometimes grammatical mistakes.

heading: 3.3.1 Image-Description Datasets
content: Descriptions tell exactly what is seen in the image. They are normally referring to the objects present, their attributes, any action or the type of the scene. Pascal1K dataset [1] (Rashtchian et al., 2010) is used is tasks involving classification and detection. The  dataset has only 20 classes with subjects ranging from animals to bridges and buildings. This is because no filter has been applied to improve the data, resulting in random data and sometimes complex concepts. Flickr8K dataset [2]  (Hodosh et al., 2013) c ontains selected images for particular actions and objects. Since these are not some randomly collected images, but selected on the requests of user. Flickr8k contain five descriptions against each image. The descriptions are collected through the Amazon M echanical Turk, which is a trademark itself for getting authentic and good quality annotations from a large number of people. Nevertheless, the dataset is still filtered further, resulting in a small but good quality dataset

heading: 3.3.2 Image-Caption Datasets
content: These d atasets have captions against the images, which is quite different from descriptions. Captions are not exactly identifying the entities or the objects in the image, rather it verbalises the concepts that cannot be seen in the image.

heading: MS COCO
content: This is known as one of the more richer datasets with almost 328,000 images and over 2500,000 instances. The categories are less as compared with the number of instances. Apart from the large amount of data, this is a rich dataset on terms of its labelling and segmentat ion. It identifies each and every one of the instances present in the image and classifies them accordingly. Another advantage of this dataset is that it does not focus only on the main subject in the image, but objects that are partially or fully visible in the background are also extracted and identified. In short, it is better to call it a scene dataset, rather than an image dataset.

It is a different kind of a dataset from all the typical datasets mentioned above. The images are acquired from Flickr and annotated by users, but the thing that differentiates them from other datasets is that it is web scaled and is updated on a regular basis.

heading: 4 Base-Line Model
content: With the amount of work that has been done for the image captioning task, it was a difficult decision to select one model for experimentation and implementation purposes. Such a model was required that applies state of the art architecture, easily implementable and easily evaluated. The quality of the captions produced by the model should also be good and accurate. In short, choosing a perfect image captioning model as our base-line was the plan.

heading: 4.1 Introduction
content: For the purpose of obtaining single sentence captions, the model that we have selected is based on the works of Karpathy et al [1 ]. The model is a deep neural network that learns an alignment between text and the visual image it describes. Since two modalities are involved, this is a multimodal architecture, meaning it can caption a query image, as well as retrieve images against a query sentence. This model produces state of the art captions that outperform other approaches.

heading: 4.2 Architecture
content: Karpathy applies the encoder-decoder architecture on this model.  The alignment between the two modalities (image regions and the textual description  against it) is done by using a structured objective. For the modalities to be aligned, they need to associate, or mapped in a common space. The model by Karpathy at el. links the two modalities through a common  space called multimodal embedding space and a structured objective. The model as achieved the of the art results in image retrieval through this multimodal embedding. Basically, a multimodal Recurrent Neural Network architecture takes an input image and generates its description in text. The experiments show that the generated sentences meaningfully beat retrieval based baseline models present up to date. The model produces sensible qualitative predictions. We then train the model on the inferred correspondences and evaluate its performance on a new dataset of region -level annotations.

heading: 5.1 Introduction
content: Rather than generating one sentence that captions the image, Johnson et al [1] propose a model which generates multiple sentences describing an image. Although the architecture that is used is almost identical to our base line model and has almost the same encoding -decoding techniques, it cannot be labelled as an image captioning task. Some images and their generated descriptions are shown in section 5.3 which will better explain this point. For extracting the image regions, a CNN model, having a novel dense localisation layer, is used. Then, a RNN language models used which takes the identified labels and generates sentences based on them. The training is done on the Visual Genome dataset, which is a huge dataset and contains multiple descriptions against each image. This allows the model to be more ‘imaginative’ and have more ‘vocabulary’ although the descriptions vary in size, it is wrong to think that it can produce novel descriptions.

heading: 5.2 Architecture
content: The first phase is extracting image regions from the input and outputting a vector representation to be passed on to the localisation layer, which is the second phase. Each of the regions are identified and labelled. labels with multiple sentences. An interpolation technique is applied that allows the propagate gradients backward through the coordinates of predicted regions. Lastly, a language model using RNN is applied to retrieve similar descriptions from the dataset.

heading: Region Extraction
content: A VGG -16 CNN architecture [41] is used for extracting image regions. It consists o f 13 convolutional layers along with 5 pooling layers. The final layer is removed from this pre -trained model, resulting in an encoding of the image at fixed, defined image locations.

heading: Localization Layer
content: The encoding of the input image is received by the localisation layer which identifies the regions of interests and extracts a representation from each region. The trick is that the representations are all of the same and fixed size, localising the input tensor completely. Against the regions of interest, three output tensors each are returned: coordinates tensor, which gives the coordinates of the bounding box; the score tensor gives the confidence score for each region and the features tensor represents the features of each region in the output.

heading: 6 Experiments
content: Experiments that primarily work on improving or enhancing the overall performance of a model, are merited high. Some experiments are conducted as comparative studies, and some are conducted for enhancing. In the case of an image -captioning model, there are quite a lot of things to play around with. The encoder has a CNN with many hidden layers. Removing and adding layers to the CNN can result in different features of the image to be extracted, and hence different captions. Same is the case on the encoding phase where one can specify their own beam size or re -rank the captions according to some pre-defined criteria. So, naturally, the priority of this work was on  improving the model’s performance in terms of caption quality and accuracy. Unfortunately, making changes in the architecture was not feasible on an average computer. Even if one uses a high-end GPU, it takes days and sometimes even weeks to re-train a model, as mentioned in the work of Vinyals et al. [1 ] which states that training their image captioning model takes about a month to train. We aimed to do the following through our experiments: 1) Evaluate our base line model from Section 4 for caption quality and accuracy, and compare the captions produced against another state of the art model MS -API [2] Section 6.1 describes this evaluation and comparative study in detail. 2) Enhance the quality of captions generated by the models discussed in Section 4 and Section 5 by changing possible parameter values (in the encoding phase only). 3) Compare the difference in metric scores when using a single reference sentence against the scores computed when using multiple references., and suggest a novel method of producing number of reference sentences without any human effort required.

heading: 6.1 Evaluation
content: The evaluation of machine generated caption is a great challenge (discussed in Section 1). Traditionally, this task is performed by experts who carefully analyse the structure, saliency, accuracy and correctness of the generated caption against the image. But hiring experts is expensive and can take a lot of time. On the other hand, the automatic metrics are very handy and can evaluate thousands of captions in a minute, but are not known for their consistency. The approach we implement uses both human judgment scores and the metric scores to find the correlation between them. Since the captions from the multi-descriptions generator are redundant and large in number, evaluating them is not advisable through the techniques mentioned. They are only for evaluati ng one caption per image. So, the evaluation section focuses only on the base -model proposed by Karpathy. In the first phase of our evaluation, we present a “Consensus -based” human evaluation system (section 6.1.1) through which we gather robust human judg ement scores against the captions that that are being evaluated. In the second phase, we evaluate the same captions mathematically, using automatic metrics.

heading: 6.1.1 Consensus-based human evaluation
content: We designed an online survey to collect human ratings for our set of Candidate Captions (CC). The set consists of a hundred images, each of which is captioned by our baseline model. We presented all the image-caption pairs to a group of people and told them to evaluate the captions. Obviously, a hundred images are a lo t for a person to rate, and that alone in one sitting. A way around has to be there for evaluations involving thousands of data -items or images. Multiple methods are applied to get a uniform human score that, even if have some outliers, the overall score doesn’t change much. In this case each image is rated by three different people ensuring that there is no biasness. The three scores are averaged to give a ‘consensus based’ score for one image. This way, you have the opportunity to know the total average score given to the model. Before the start of the survey, the evaluators were given clear and easy to understand instructions regarding their role. The instructions also included a thorough understanding of our rating scale. (1-5) and the critical way in which they have to tackle the presented task. We made sure that each image was rated by at least five people, so that we obtain a consensus based, averaged human score. A screenshot is shown in Figure taken from the survey. The evaluators were told to rate a  single caption on its 1) Quality, refers to the overall correctness and fluency and 2) Accuracy which refers to its precision.

Score of 4: The caption describes the image quiet well, but with grammatical mistakes. Score of 3: The caption almost describes the image (minor mistakes allowed e.g. in the number of entities). Score of 2: The caption only describes some aspects of the image with grammatical mistakes as well. Score of 1: The caption bears no relation to the image.

heading: 6.2 Metrics evaluation
content: For metric evaluation, a set of ground-truth is required against which the candidate captions can be compared. As explained before, Ground-truth (GT) needs to be as much accurate and correct as possible. Since it acts as the reference set in metric evaluation, the more robust the set of ground truth is, the better the evaluation scores will be.

heading: Candidate Captions Set:
content: This set contains those captions that are produced by our base-line method. As these are the captions that we are primarily evaluating, the metrics will be using this set and compare it against the Ground-Truth Set. For comparison purposes, we will be taking one more candidate captions set, comprising of captions produced by another automatic image captioning model, MS-APIBOT. For the same 100 images, our problem set, we obtain captions from both models.

heading: Ground-Truth Set:
content: This is the set against which the candidate captions are to be compared. Since this is basically a reference set, it needs to consist of captions that are accurate and annotated by humans.  Keeping this in mind, an analysis of different datasets was conducted, with the aim of selecting the dataset containing daily life random images along with one or more sentences describing the respected image. Many people have proposed such datasets, but the dataset presented by (Hodosh et al., 2013) [3]  is perfect for the job. The dataset contains almost 8000 image s all of which are representing specific objects and actions. Our problem set, the images against which we generated captions for evaluation, consists of 100 randomly chosen images from this dataset. The datasets consist of five descriptions per image, which are obtained through crowd -sourcing from the Amazon Mechanical Turk [ 2]. AMT is a payed service where one can get human annotations on a large scale. The quality of descriptions in the dataset is quite good and can be observed that they are already filtered out. Nonetheless, we still post-process the descriptions that we need (descriptions for images in our problem set) by passing it through a spell check, and looking for any grammatical error present that could be manually removed. And voila! We arrive at our first set of ground -truths GT(a) This set includes five descriptions per image, which are human annotated and checked and rechecked for any error or mistake. For evaluating purposes, we further use human judgment to rank each of the five sentences i n GT(a). The highest ranked sentence for each image is selected, and so we arrive at our second set of ground-truth GT(b).

heading: 6.2.1 Implementation
content: All the automatic metrics use similar methodology to compute their respected scores i.e. a set of candidate sentences (which are being evaluated) compared against a set of ground -truths, or the reference sentences. For analysis purposes, we divide this experiment into two parts. The first part evaluates the machine generated captions (candida te) against GT(a). The second evaluates generated captions against the second set of ground –truths GT(b). Figure illustrates example of GT(a) and GT(b) for an image. Since we are actually talking about caption quality, rather than sentence quality, the me trics have to be carefully selected. Some of the metrics used to evaluate machine generated captions are not even designed for the purpose. Since human judgments are expensive and time -consuming to collect, we now examine how well they can be approximated by Meteor and Cider. The caption generated by baseline model (Karpathy et al.) and test model (MS-Caption) is compared with our 5 Ground truth reference captions.  we cannot assume that the generated caption is identical to one of the reference captions. We therefore examine to what extent Meteor and Cider scores agree with human judgments when the candidate pool contains machine generated captions. The captions generated by baseline model (Karpathy et al.) and test model (MS -CaptionBot) is compared with our Ground truth reference GT(a) and then with GT(B). When calculating Meteor, if more than one reference sentence is available, the candidate sentence is  scored against each reference independently, and the pair with the highest score is selected. Cider simply compares the candidate sentence to all the reference captions and gives the score accordingly.

heading: 6.3 Enhancement
content: Changing the architecture of an image captioning model to enhance the captions quality is beyond this project’s scope.  Such exper iments require the staging of complex algorithms, high -end machines and a lot of time. Instead we make enhancements in the encoding part, where there is no re-training required after a change. The encoder is only responsible for retrieval task in our model, so we arrive at our first general hypothesis: The quality of captions in terms of retrieval, or the accuracy by which the retrieved images are similar to the query image, can be manipulated.

heading: 6.3.1 Beam Search
content: Since our base-line model from Section 4 is based on the encoding decoding technique, we start by looking at the parameters we could change. Beam Size is a parameter that is used in the decoding phase. It is a pre -defined value that selects the top retrieved captions and feed them back to the model. The t op-predictions are once again checked by the model, re -ranked and fed back again. This ensures that the top ranked predictions would always be on the top. To enhance the quality of the retrieved captions, for our base-line model, we manipulated the beam size and evaluated the captions generated for each. Starting from beam size b=2 and all the way to beam size b=5 we produced four Candidate Captions Set and compare them individually using Bleu and ROUGE_L. Bleu measures the precision while ROUGE_L measures the recall. Since these two metrics are for measuring these two properties specifically, we use them here.   The beam size having the best evaluation scores against its generated captions set is thus identified as the Optimised Beam Size. Figure illustrates an example image and along with its caption at different beam sizes.

heading: 6.3.2 Reranking Captions
content: The multi sentence generator model, against one image retrieves hundreds of captions which is found to be redundant and contains a relatively big number of identical captions in terms of textual similarity. Thus, it is relevant to reduce the set while maintaining the conveyed information. For the sake of our experiment, we limit the retrieved captions at R=50. After the captions are retrieved, we rank the captions according to their Confidence. Figure shows two images along with their bounding -boxes, the caption for each bounding -box and the confidence score ( C) against each c aption. The confidence is the score given to each of the bounding-box in an image. It is a probabilistic value which tells about the ‘confidence’ of the particular caption retrieved from the training set against the bounding -box. After manually analyzing the confidences against each caption, we decide to select the captions with Confidence C >= 0. After the captions have been filtered and ranked according to their confidence, we select the top seven captions from each image, and hence come up with our own data set. We name our dataset as Densely Annotated dataset, which is further explained in section 7

heading: Optimum Beam Size
content: The first improvement that is suggested by is to use beam -size=2 for this model. Out of the five beam-sizes captions evaluated and analysed, the optimum beam is identified. For the model to be implemented on the web, this optimum size has been chosen. Since Bleu and ROUGE_L compute their score by comparing sentence to sentence, rather than multiple re ference sentences, we use GT(b) as the set of reference captions. Table: beam-search results For measuring precision between the generated caption and the reference caption, we selected BLEU(overall) which is the geometric mean of  BLEU 1,2,3 and 4 altogether. Table shows that with beam-size=2, the BLEU value is the highest, meaning it gives the most precise captions. As the beam-size increases, the precook is seen to be decreasing. To measure the recall, ROUGE_L was selected. In th is case, once again, the captions produced with beam-size=2 got the highest results. Concretely, this establishes the fact that in terms of both precision and recall, using beam-size=2 is the best possible beam-search parameter. Use of Multiple Reference Captions: The point of conducting the same experiments against GT(a) and then GT(b) was to prove that more reference sentences result in better evaluation results. This evident from the results obtained when GT(a) was used, which consists of five reference captions. We suggest that the more captions are in the set of reference sentences, the more authentic the evaluation will be. Beam Size  BLEU ROUGE L

heading: Densely Annotated Dataset
content: In Section 6, we described how we filtered out the top-ranked retrieved captions from the multi- sentence generation model. We then selected the top seven captions and named it our Densely Annotated Dataset. Figure shows an image along with the seven captions showing the quality and accuracy of the new dataset. This method of obtaining accurate descriptions against images is much more easier and cheaper than obtaining descriptions from humans. To obtain descriptions from humans, it is required to pay a group of people or hire the services of platforms like the Amazon Mechanical Turk which can be both time-taking and expensive. Alternatively, the dataset that we have proposed does the same thing, i.e. it generates multiple captions that are almost human like. It should be kept in mind that although automatic metrics don’t require a lot of human effort, but there is the problem of obtaining ground -truths. The ground truth needs to be as much accurate a caption as possible, and that is why those captions are considered ground truths which are written or agreed upon by humans. Obtaining them can require human effort and time and so the process cannot be called fully automatic. We suggest a method in which the ground-truth can be considered as the Densely Annotated Dataset. This is feasible because first of all, these captions are written by humans basically, and the model just uses them to caption novel images. Secondly, a large number of captions can be obtained, satisfying the argument about using more reference sentences for evaluation.

heading: 60 of 63  09 January 2018
content: Training own model: Both models that we discussed and implement in this project use a pre-trained model to classify the objects. The pre -trained model is basically a Convolutional Neural Network named VGG -16 trained on different datasets. Due to the amount and quality of the training data, we can see that the performance of the models is not up to the mark. Making changes in the hyperparamet ers of the encoding model, or training it ourselves based on some domain -specific task, can eliminate the problem of over-fitting and give more promising results. Improvements in Human Evaluation: To obtain human judgements for our experiments, we used people from our university to get them to score the captions. These people, although well-educated and fluent in the English language, were no expert judges. Better human evaluation results may be obtained if we use people who have any kind of prior experience in the evaluation of  image captioning . While we averaged three peoples’ score for generating the score of one image, using more people can give more accurate results. Also, a better option is using a 4-point scale, with simpler options like ‘bad, ‘okay’, ‘good and ‘excellent’.

heading: 8 Conclusion
content: Through this project, we discussed the task of automatic image captioning, especially in the light of Neural Networks. Showing our understanding of this hugel y complex but interesting field was a large part of our project, and how these networks finally converge to the main concept of our project: Artificial Cognition. We then elaborated on the different models and techniques that are presently available for this task. The different datasets available and the evaluating techniques used are also presented to give a clear understanding of the experiments that we conducted. We have also presented the drawbacks associated with each method and technique After a complete analysis, we identified the best approach and selected two models based on that architecture. Next, we discussed the two selected models and give a qualitative and quantitative analysis on both of them. Our analysis shows that, although the two models are state-of-the-art and efficient in their working, the quality of the captions they produce fall short when corelated with human scores. The same problem is identified in the automatic metrics that are used for mathematically evaluating the captions quality. A need is indicated for improvements. The captions from the first model, which generates one caption per image, are optimized by experimentally finding out the best Beam Size and them implementing the model with that particular beam size. The captions from the second model are found to be redundant, in terms that it produces hundreds and hundreds of captions per image. The captions are found to be very much descriptive and accurate, but all of them are short and identical to the captions in the datas et. Keeping in mind its limitations and forthcomings, we try to filter out the top captions for an image and thus creating our own Densely Annotated Dataset. This dataset contains only those captions that describe the image accurately and comprehensively. We point out the advantages of such a dataset and its use in evaluation purposes. Lastly, we implemented the improved model on web. Users can use the webpage to get their images captioned at real time. As compared to the previous approaches of image classification where images are annotated with a single word or a short phrase, the task of automatic image captioning is found to be more productive and useful in obtaining human -like explanations of the visual scenes around us. More research and development in this field is required and will surely lead to better Artificial Cognition systems and prove to open new possibilities for visually impaired and blind people. For the time being, even though there are many techniques that have come to light for this task , experiments show that they still fall quite short when compared with human results. This means that improvements are still required in both the captioning models and the techniques to evaluate the captions.

heading: 8.1 Future Work
content: Real-time video captioning: This was the initial motivation behind choosing this project because getting captions at real time on a smart -phone opens up countless possibilities. Alas, hardware limitation and a doubt in feasibility made us discard the idea at that time. Now, that we h ave a clearer understanding of the whole thing, the next thing to do is implementing video captioning as a useful smart -phone application. For example, combining video captioning with the GPS module in a mobile-phone, an application can be developed for visually impaired people as a navigation tool.

heading: New Datasets:
content: Before big datasets like the MS COCO or Flickr30 were introduced, most of the captioning was done using small datasets containing poor quality captions and poor-quality images. Even though improved datasets are now available, there is still place for improvements. For example, most of the datasets containing captions are annotated by different people, meaning the machine has to learn so many different ways of expression. A technique needs to be in troduced which would extract the same representation values from the whole image. New evaluation metrics: Except for the Cider metric, most of the other automatic techniques that are applied for the task of evaluating image captions are not strictly for that specific task. Some are for measuring syntactic similarity between machine translations and human translations, while others simply measure the similarity between two sentences or two paragraphs. Obviously, this is the reason for weak human correlations in our experiments since these metrics, except for Cider, although may tell about one or two features of the caption, are not suited for the job individually. Such a metric can be developed, keeping in mind the two properties required from a caption (Quality and Accuracy). The metric should be specifically for evaluating image captions and would then, surely will give a more honest correlation with human. With so many models and techniques emerging for the task of image captioning and descriptions, such a metric is in huge need right now, and would require efforts in the future.

heading: Abstract
content: This earth is our home. Humans are our family members. We cannot let anyone  sleep hungry. Let’s change the world! This project is an android application which is a platform for the people to donate daily routine extra food which they wasted in no manners. Our aim is to reduce the food waste and feed the hungry people. People can use this application to donate their foods or to collect food for the hungry people. Millions of lives are starving for food around us, have a Tap to feed a life. Let’s work together to bridge the gap and reduce hunger and food waste in our beloved country.

heading: 1 Introduction
content: FOOD DONOR is an android application that provides opportunities to people to donate food easily even they don’t need to search a hungry one. This app allows a layman to use technology for their ease in an efficient way. Integrated maps will be used in this application which automatically gets the location of the person who wants to donate food and display the location of the person who request for the food. Using location data, the app matches between the donor and a nearby organization to collect food. This app allows a layman to use technology for their ease in an efficient way. User can share the food to available Charity services.  User can find Charities near to the location and can deliver them self, user will get the root map assistance to charity which will easy to reach the location. Otherwise all the user need to do is to upload the food images in the app and immediately all the volunteers will get notification and will contact you to pick up the food and serve to charity, the user can also track the status of food up to delivery. Those who ready to act as a volunteer can register as a volunteer in the app itself and can collect food from different donors and serve to Charity.  This app includes 4 major modules Donate Food, Receive Food, Volunteer and Hunger Spot.

heading: 1.1 Objectives:
content: The Goal of our project is to implement such a system, which is expected to be: • Electronically efficient, less time consuming and free from complexities. • Change culture of bagging system. • Want to provide platform where people can easily donate/receive food. • Helps Orphan Houses to request for food efficiently. • Make the people to use the technology in a better way.

heading: 1.2 Problem Statement:
content: There is no platform for the people where they can donate food. Basically people are promoting towards technology. That is the reason why Food Donor was introduced and keep on improving day by day. “Food Donation is quiet an issue nowadays for almost every individual.” Time is major issue for most of the people in today’s era. People nowadays are so busy that sometimes they do not have enough time to donate food and they waste
their food in no sense. Food Donor will ease such problems for the people. It wil l provide them with the opportunity to donate and receive food quickly.

heading: 1.3 Assumptions and constraints:
content: The project is chartered assuming that: • An incorporated database framework will be outlined by us that will be administrated by the Ministry of Health who will keep record of each needy person who request for food. • Access to people personal information (includes phone number, CNIC etc.) • Constraints are that project will be under the policies of the university.

heading: 1.4 Project Scope:
content: Mostly people when they want  to donate some food they are in looking for some bagger to safe their food from waste while in restaurants they also waste food in daily routine. So, we want to safe the food waste and provide food to the hungry people and different food banks and differe nt NGO’s where people are feed. Internet and Smartphone is the major invention of this age and people are moving towards it very extensively so in that perspective our application will have the greatest scope in market. We are also using GPS system in our application which is the very fine feature of Smartphone so it also plays a major role in increasing the scope of our application. Our project will be covering an Android application for android devices. GPS based location service will be used in our application to get the location of the donor and receiver will be provided to that person on the basis of its current location. Food donor and receiver services will be implementing in this application.

heading: 2.1 Literature Review:
content: There are many different ways to donate food and many different apps are playing their role in order to save the wastage of food. There are many different ways to donate food that is used by the people. Usually people are in search of beggars whom which they give them extra food of daily routine. There are many people in Pakistan still wasting lots of food and there are also have some restaurants that waste food in no sense. We provide people a platform through our application where they can donate extra food of daily routine, and they make people happy by serving them food. In fast -moving time of today, when everyone is squeezed for time, the majority of people are fastidious when it comes to placing a food donate. Now -a-days people do not care of someone who is not afford food expenses and people should help them. FOOD DONOR (online donating app) that is proposed here, greatly simplifies the request for food for both the Donor and the Receiver. This app allows a layman to use technology for their ease in an efficient way. App presents an interactive and up -to-date menu with all available food in an easy to use manner. This app will be user friendly, easy to use and makes the food donating procedure more time saving and efficient. Integrated maps will be used in this application which automatically gets the location of the donor/receiver and display the requests accordingly and user also able to check the Hunger Spots. Food availability is also an issue now -a-days in food banks which will be covere d by this application. Receiver can request for 2 items per day as he wants and then the list of item will be updated. User can also view all the request details before checking out. In the end, Donor/Receiver gets request confirmation details. Once the re quest is placed it is entered in the database and retrieved in pretty much real time. This process will allow donor to quickly go through the requests as they are received and process all requests efficiently and effectively with minimum delays and disorientation.

content: The objective of unit testing is to check each & every component or code pieces of an application separately and check its working before running the whole application and testing it unit testing is performed to resolve the minor issues of an application. Components may be required to be disconnected from each other while unit testing.

heading: 4.3 Integration testing:
content: The goal of integration testing is to test the modules in an application that are connected with each other and their functionality gives a mutual unique result. Integration testing is always done after the application is done with unit testing . In integration testing all requirements are checked according to documentation. For examples: order module and admin module are connected and they give a mutual output in result. Their connection is checked by integration testing and their result is analyzed. After unit testing, we continued incorporating units to give legitimate shape to item. After every unit coordinated, we performed joining testing on our framework. heading: Abstract
content: “Stitched out” is a tailor’s management system and delivery marketplace.  It’s a project that will prove helpful for both the customer as well as the tailor.  It will also serve as an online clothes ordering system through which customers can create their accounts and store their measurements and share with the de sired tailor and they  can tailor fit clothes for them. People can also choose cloth from different brands and ask them to be tailored. It will also provide delivery and pickup scheduling, order placement features as well.  As for the tailors, the site will help them manage their customers. “Stitched Out” will also provide its services to the brand vendors. The vendors can create their accounts and promote their products. They can also promote the sales, promotions and discounts offered by their respected brands.

heading: 1.1 Introduction
content: In this modern era, almost everyone tries to find a way to ease their lives. The workload has increased exceptionally and a person always jumps at the opportunity to ease their life anyway they can. “Stitched Out” is that kind of innovative idea which can reduce the load off the shoulders of its customers. “Stitched out” will provide a platform to the tailors, the customers as well as the brands (vendors). “Stitched Out” is a user friendly site which will help the user on every step of the process. A person using the site will simply have to identify themselves as the customer, tailor or vendor. After that, they will mak e their account, providing the site with valid information. A  customer can simply input their measurements in the site and choose the type of brand and cloth they want to be tailored and these values can be updated (If the user wants)  later on.  The custome r can update their measurements and address anytime they want just by a click. The customer has complete control of the brand they want to choose, the cloth they want as well as the tailor they want to work on their clothes. The notification will be send to the customer and tailor for giving/receiving the order. The website will work as a platform for every person who want their cloths to be tailored. It will also serve as a clothing marketplace and clothes from different brands will be available here. The products of different brands will be given for the customer to browse through.  The customer can buy clothes from there and assign it to the tailor as per customer choice. The tailor will follow the address of the customer, bring over the cloth and will start doing his job. The tailor will inform the customer as soon as he is done with the stitching. From there on out, it will depend on the customer whether they want the clothes to be delivered or they will pick them up themselves. As for the tailors, they will have to identify themselves and make an account as well just like the customers but with some different information. The site will ask for their specialities (Suit, Qameez&Shalwar and Kurta etc.) and will categorize them as such. The tailors will have  access to their personal information. They can update their speciality as well as the cost of each. The y can also see their rating they have served. The tailors will have access to a notification panel as well as a tab where the previous orders will be shown. All the orders are shown that are received by the tailors in the received order tab. The details of customers are shown in the order descriptions .The tailors will bring over the cloth (if any) themselves and start their work. Once the stitching of the clothes is complete, the tailor will inform the customer and the customer will decide whether to get their clothes delivered or they will pick it up themselves. The vendors (brands) will have their own module. The user will identify the role “Brand” and will create their account. The functionalities of the vendors are quite simple. They can  add their products with appropriate details and browse them if they want to update anything. They can also remove old products from their catalogue. The vendors will also receive orders from the customers. The pending orders will appear on the vendors account.

heading: 1.2 Objective
content: “Stitched Out” will provide an excellent service in this modern era of communication and it will be a huge timesaver. Clothes are part of our life and no matter what era it is, clothes will be always required by everyone. People can buy readymade clothes but given the di fferent build of each individual, they don’t always fit. Ultimately people turn to tailors to get fit clothes. “Stitched out” will allow the users to simply give their  measurements and cloths through an easy process. They won’t have to hassle with buying the cloth and going to the tailor. All they have to do is give their required information and sit back till their cloths are tailored. This will help in decreasing road usage and traffic congestion as people won’t have to travel unnecessarily. It will take the load of shopping off every individual so they can focus on their jobs or other activities. It will open new job and business avenues . “Stitched Out” will  recommend the tailors  to other customers as they will be rated by the customers who have availed their services. This could also help in advertising certain uprising tailors. It can reduce the work load of customers as they won’t have to shop for cloths and the delivery person can drop off their packages to their homes

heading: Critical Analysis
content: Stitch-My-Fabric provides the customer with an online store where they can easily get their clothes tailored. They also provide delivery and pick up services for the clothes. They don’t give direct access to the brands to the customers so that they can but their clothes. The customer has to access the brand’s website separately. The customer has to buy the cloth form any online store and in the deliver address of the cloth, the customer has to put the address of Stitch -My- Fabric’s store. Once the customer has done so, the website will ask for the customer’s order number and the measurements and other  required details. They also don’t have several tailors. The customer cannot select from a list of tailors and they only sew women clothes.

heading: Introduction
content: Stitch-to-Fit is a very simple website with online booking and clothes delivery system. They provide the customer with a representative who visits the customer’s personal address and acquires all the required information. They stitch the clothes within 7 -8 days and personally hand deliver to the customer’s given address.

heading: Critical Analysis
content: Stitch-to-Fit is a very simple website. They have provided their phone number for the customers to call and book their services. Once the customer is booked, they send their representative to the customer’s given address. The representative will take the customer’s measurements as well as other information regarding the style of the clothes. The clothes should be available at the customer’s home when the representative is to visit so that he can take the clothes back to their store with him. Once the sewing i s done, the representative will deliver the clothes to the customer’s given address. They don’t have an online store, just a website with a phone number. They don’t provide 24 -hour service as their representative has specific working hours. They don’t give access to any online brand for the customer to purchase clothes from.

The customer has to place an online order, schedule a pickup time and leave the rest to them. They will pick up the customer’s cloth, sew it and will deliver it to the customer’s given address.
